#2666. MLB offseason bold predictions: Tarik Skubal breaks records, World Series champ gets a deal, a FA frenzy, more

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

With the Brewers crowned World Series champions, the 2026-27 offseason is underway. We're still waiting for the first significant free agent signing or trade, which isn't unusual less than a week into the offseason. Give it another week or so and the action will pick up. Before the hot stove really gets burning, here are 10 bold predictions for the 2026-27 offseason. Remember, all geniuses were called crazy at first.

Yoshinobu Yamamoto's $325 million deal with the Dodgers is the largest pitching contract in history, and our first bold prediction says Tarik Skubal, this offseason's undisputed No. 1 free agent, will beat that. Specifically, he'll sign a contract that is closer to $400 million in value than $300 million, which is another way of saying he'll clear $350 million and break Yamamoto's record for total dollars by a good bit. Scott Boras, Skubal's agent, likes to break contract records with room to spare, not just by a tiny bit. Skubal is the best free agent starter since Yamamoto, and the best free agent starter with MLB experience since Gerrit Cole in 2019. It's a very thin free agent class with few places to (wisely) spend money. The bet here is a team steps up and gives Skubal a record deal.

Milwaukee's thing over the last few years has been trading its top players a year before free agency (Corbin Burnes, Freddy Peralta, Devin Williams, etc.) and obviously it has worked for them. William Contreras is at that point now: he's scheduled to hit the open market next offseason. This next bold prediction says the Brewers will buck that trend and instead sign the World Series MVP to a long-term extension that keeps him in Milwaukee for at least another few years, if not the rest of his career. How does six years at $24 million a pop sound? That would be $144 million total and the richest contract given to a catcher in the last 13 years, clearing Will Smith's $140 extension with the Dodgers. The World Series champs keep their most irreplaceable player. It has been foretold.

Every offseason is important, and this one is extra important for new Astros GM Randy Flores, who must figure out what to do with third baseman Isaac Paredes and shortstop Jeremy Peña, both a year away from free agency. Keeping Peña and trading Paredes, and installing Carlos Correa at the hot corner, is the sensible move. This bold prediction says the opposite will happen. The Astros will trade Peña and keep Paredes, and figure out their 2027 infield alignment later. Houston needs help up and down the roster, particularly on the mound, and I think the offers for Peña will simply be too great for Flores to ignore. It will be similar to the Kyle Tucker trade two years ago. The Astros don't have to move Peña, but the offers will get to a point where they just can't say no.

On one hand, keeping the offense intact and adding some pitching would be a viable offseason plan for the Braves. On the other hand, can they really run it back with the same offense that flatlined after June 1 and in the NLDS? It might be time to shake things up a bit, and I boldly predict it will happen. Ronald Acuña Jr., Drake Baldwin, Michael Harris II, and Matt Olson aren't going anywhere. No team will take the current version of Austin Riley and the six years (!) remaining on his contract. That leaves Ozzie Albies and I suppose Sean Murphy, though the latter is well into role player status now. Does that make this bold prediction a "the Braves will trade Albies" prediction? Yeah, I guess it does. It feels like things are getting a little stale in Atlanta and it's time to change up a core.

You could argue Freddy Peralta is the second-best free agent starter behind Skubal. You could also argue it's Trevor Rogers, who doesn't have Peralta's pedigree or track record, but has strong under-the-hood performance indicators, the kind that project well into the future and get players paid. So, for this bold prediction, I'll say that Rogers signs a richer deal than Peralta, even though the latter is the more famous player and has been better in their careers to date. It'll be close. I can see Rogers getting something in the $125 million range and Peralta signing for right around $120 million, but, in the end, Rogers will sign for more guaranteed dollars because he's a year and a half younger and teams love nothing more than players they believe have untapped upside. That's Rogers, not Peralta.

After the Dodgers swept in the NLCS, there were calls to infuse some youth into the roster, and, honestly, they need it. Fortunately, Los Angeles has one of the best prospects in the game in the precocious Josue De Paula, who was so impressive late in the season. Trading an outfielder to clear a spot for De Paula seems like such an obvious move that I'm not sure this prediction qualifies as bold. Andy Pages and Kyle Tucker aren't going anywhere, which leaves Teoscar Hernández. How about a trade that sends Hernández back to the Blue Jays? It's a one-year commitment, the Blue Jays badly need over-the-fence power, and the fan base already loves the guy. Teoscar to Toronto as what amounts to their George Springer replacement. I boldly predict it.

Every offseason, there are two teams that appear to match up so well that a trade feels inevitable. Last offseason, it was the Brewers and Mets for a Freddy Peralta deal. This offseason, it's the Cubs and Yankees. The Cubs need rotation help and have some young position players to spare (like Matt Shaw). The Yankees need infield help and have starting pitching to trade (like Will Warren). I'm not saying Shaw for Warren will happen or even should happen. I'm just saying Chicago's and New York's trade chips and roster needs align very well, and when that happens, a trade typically comes together. This bold prediction says the Cubs will send a position player to the Yankees for a starting pitcher, with maybe some other pieces involved on both sides.

There are trade rumors involving a Mariners starting pitcher every offseason and there's a good reason for that. They have a lot of really good starters and teams want them. The Mariners currently have Kade Anderson, Logan Gilbert, Emerson Hancock, George Kirby, Bryce Miller, and Bryan Woo lined up for their 2027 rotation. They could keep them all because pitching depth has a way of disappearing, sure, but Seattle needed another bat even before Randy Arozarena became a free agent. This next bold prediction says the Mariners finally trade one of their starters in an arm-for-bat deal. I'll say Kirby, who is two years away from free agency, is the one to go. Gilbert is a one-year rental but the better pitcher. The others all have longer control than Kirby.

After coming out of the gate so well in April and May, Munetaka Murakami finished right where the pundits expected. He hit .207 and had the highest strikeout rate among qualified hitters, but he also slugged 35 home runs in only 127 games. Hanshin Tigers third baseman Teruaki Sato, who will be posted for MLB teams this offseason, is similar to Murakami as a strikeout-prone lefty with huge power. This bold prediction says Sato will double Murakami's contract with the White Sox (two years and $34 million) because he's a better bet to stay at third base, a position that is barren in free agency, and because Murakami provided proof of concept. He showed that a player with big contact concerns in Japan can indeed succeed stateside, even if it is an eyesore at times. Four years and $68 million for Sato, perhaps with an opt out that makes the $68 million not really $68 million.

Dec. 1 is of course when the collective bargaining agreement expires and the owners are expected to lock out the players. My final bold prediction says free agents and teams will get out ahead of the potential lockout and sign in November. Players won't want to wait until who knows when to sign and teams will want to lock in contracts so they can be grandfathered into whatever the next CBA brings. MLB free agency tends to be slow-moving. Last offseason, only one of our top 10 free agents signed in November, and that was Shota Imanaga taking the qualifying offer. Only three other top 10 free agents signed in December. The other six signed on Jan. 14 or later. This offseason will be the opposite, I boldly predict. There will be a flurry of activity in November and at least seven of our top 10 free agents will put pen to paper before a potential lockout.

#2665. 2026 NFL trade deadline tracker: Latest deals, grades as Jordan Davis heads to Jacksonville

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

A steady stream of blockbuster moves in advance of the 2026 NFL trade deadline redistributed some of the league's top talent at numerous positions. Even more impactful transactions could be on the way before Nov. 10, but in the meantime, the Chicago Bears are the biggest winners of the deadline thus far with their highly fruitful acquisition of Jeffery Simmons, the Jacksonville Jaguars are the most aggressive buyers with their pursuit of a host of defensive players and the Indianapolis Colts emerged as the most aggressive sellers in dealing Quenton Nelson and DeForest Buckner.

Trade watch continues for a myriad of stars on struggling teams, including Jonathan Taylor, Khalil Mack, George Pickens and others. At the same time, teams battling for position at the front of the postseason race must decide how much to invest in those standouts who are available on the trade market.

There is only one more game until the trade deadline, so this year's contenders and pretenders are about as clear as they will be before it is too late to buy and sell. It is safe to expect a flurry of moves in the next 24 hours as those franchises gear up for the home stretch or look ahead to the future.

Below is every in-season trade ahead of the NFL's 2026 deadline.

Just when it seemed like the Jaguars had filled all of their needs, they went out and made their biggest move of all. Jacksonville's acquisition of Davis is a blockbuster in every sense of the word. The standout defensive tackle will be on the team's books through 2029 after signing a lucrative contract extension with the Eagles earlier this year and will be among the faces of the franchise as it pursues its first Super Bowl. His arrival marks the third trade for a defensive player in one day for Jacksonville and gives them a star in the trenches who should make an already superb group even more impenetrable.

On the other side, Philadelphia is officially in tear-down mode for 2026. Nothing signals a rebuild like moving a foundational player months after locking him into a new contract. The Eagles now have 10 picks in the first two rounds of the next three drafts and can seek an expedited return to playoff contention with a couple of massive draft day hauls.

The Lions should be better off than they were before in the defensive backfield with the addition of Cisco, but by how much? Cisco arrives in a unit that ranks dead last in stopping the pass at 260.9 yards per game. He slipped from his status as an every-week starter and was at the top of the Jets' depth chart for just four of nine games this season. While he remains productive, this is not a home-run transaction for a Detroit team that has to be better on his side of the ball in order to achieve its goals. This could age much better if and when Kerby Joseph returns to the lineup, because Cisco would be a pleasant depth option behind both Joseph and Brian Branch.

New York will have to wait a year to reap the benefits of this trade. It is a success to get something in return for a player who started fewer than half of his games this season, but the Jets need all the draft capital they can stockpile in order to pull themselves out of their rebuild, and 2028 is a long way away.

Jacksonville entered the week with needs at safety and defensive tackle and filled both of them in a matter of hours. Shortly after acquiring Jessie Bates III, the Jaguars made a play for Godchaux, boosting a defense that may already be Super Bowl-caliber. This is a necessary addition for general manager James Gladstone after he watched DaVon Hamilton go down with a torn quad in Week 8 and one that should keep the NFL's No. 5 run defense in the top echelon.

The pick heading to New Orleans will become a 2027 sixth-round pick if the Jaguars acquire one, according to ESPN. They do not currently own one but are projected to receive two compensatory sixth-round picks, according to Spotrac. Even with the caveat on the return, the Saints upgraded in the deal considering they spent a seventh-rounder to acquire Godchaux in a trade last year. He was a questionable fit in a run defense that ranks fifth-worst in the NFL, anyway.

The Jaguars secured a rental for their secondary and an impactful one at that. Bates is a perennial All-Pro safety who not only beefs up the starting lineup with renowned playmaking ability but also adds depth to a group that is dealing with injuries and just lost Eric Murray for the year with an elbow issue. Jacksonville is right in the midst of its contention window and is in play for the AFC's No. 1 seed, so any move that strengthens its Super Bowl chances is justifiable, even if it gives up quite a bit in the way of draft picks to pull it off.

Those picks make this deal a beneficial one for the Falcons, too. Atlanta should have expected to lose Bates in free agency this coming offseason, since he was not among the many players it extended this past summer. The second-round pick is better than any compensatory pick that would have come with his departure, and the 2028 fifth-rounder sweetened the deal even further. Now is the time for the Falcons to turn expiring contracts into future assets, because, at 3-6, they are unlikely to contend for anything beyond a potential first-place finish in the NFL's weakest division.

Baltimore agreed to trade for Cardinals QB Jacoby Brissett and completed the deal over the weekend after its "Thursday Night Football" loss. This was an expected move for the Ravens, because their quarterback situation went from bad to worse in Week 8. The highly anticipated return of starter Lamar Jackson lasted just one play. Jackson suffered a thumb injury and is now on injured reserve. Tyler Huntley, who started in place of Jackson, took over but also went down. He is out for the season with a turf toe injury. The team relied on emergency third quarterback Joe Fagnano to finish the game and started him on Thursday.

Brissett spent the last two seasons with the Cardinals, who benched him in his final game with the team and turned instead to Gardner Minshew. The return of draft capital for a quarterback who lost his job, was unhappy all offseason about his contract situation and projected as a bridge to an eventual first-round pick is a huge success for a rebuilding Arizona team.

In giving up two first-rounders to secure a perennial All-Pro defensive tackle, the Bears went all-in and opened their Super Bowl contention window. The transaction paid immediate dividends when Simmons logged a sack and led the team with six tackles in his Chicago debut: A commanding 34-17 road win over the Seahawks. Mortgaging so much of their future first-round capital showed that the Bears trust their roster, as currently constructed, to compete at the top of the league, and Simmons is the kind of game-changing talent worth the steep price. His production in the pass rush and in run defense could help Chicago maximize its high-octane unit on the other side of the ball led by Caleb Williams.

This move sends the Titans deeper into their rebuild. Questions lie ahead about whether to stick with Cam Ward at quarterback, and with the first-round picks they acquired from dealing Simmons, there will be curiosity as to whether they will use one to land a new signal-caller. Regardless of how they use the picks, moving on from one of the greatest players in franchise history shows how bleak the present is in Tennessee and that all eyes are on the future.

The seemingly nonstop onslaught of injuries hit the 49ers' defensive line, resulting in CJ West landing on injured reserve with a bone chip in his knee and Alfred Collins being ruled out for the year with a torn patellar tendon. That heightened the need for immediate help in the trenches, so the 49ers brought Buckner back after his six-plus years in Indianapolis. The 49ers selected Buckner in the first round of the 2016 draft, and the best years of his prime came during his time in San Francisco, so this is a welcome return for someone the franchise remembers fondly. Buckner remains one of the NFL's top pass-rushing interior defensive linemen and will aid in the 49ers' Super Bowl push.

Buckner's exit marked the second trade in one day for the slumping Colts, who are in the midst of tearing things down with multiple star players on the move and former general manager Chris Ballard out the door. There is an argument to be made that a Day 3 pick was an underwhelming return, but for a 32-year-old veteran on an expiring contract, the Colts were content to get at least something of value for a player who was likely to leave in free agency anyway. Buckner grew publicly frustrated with Indianapolis' struggles, which heightened the anticipation for his trade or an eventual departure at the end of his contract.

Seahawks general manager Jon Schneider is keen to make big-time moves ahead of the trade deadline. This is the fourth consecutive year in which Seattle made a play for an impactful midseason addition to its roster. Nelson is as stellar of an offensive lineman as there is on the trade market this year as a six-time All-Pro and should elevate a struggling Seahawks run game over the long term, even if his arrival did not deliver an immediate boost in the loss to the Bears in his debut. This is also a savvy transaction for the front office given that it stands to receive at least one compensatory third-round pick in 2027; trading a third-rounder for Nelson was thus an easy price to pay.

The Colts got more in return for Nelson than they did for Buckner, which is to be expected considering his status as perhaps the top interior lineman in football. This is still a discount, though, and they remain without a first-round pick in either of the next two drafts. If they can use the third-rounder and next year's fifth-rounder to move up in the order, the trade deadline sale could prove more worthwhile.

Harrison reunited with his college quarterback, C.J. Stroud, upon his arrival in Houston. Will that help him rekindle what has become a disappointing career? His first two games with the Texans were mostly underwhelming, but he did haul in a touchdown reception in Week 7 and could secure a more sizable target share as the team seeks for a go-to No. 2 option behind star pass-catcher Nico Collins. This is trending toward a lost season for the Texans, but they will have another year of control over Harrison and the option to pick up a fifth year in 2028. If they can mold him into the star he was supposed to become out of Ohio State, their passing game will be in excellent shape over the long haul.

Trading Harrison was an admission that he was a bust of a former first-round pick, but to get a second-rounder in the process and to upgrade with a Day 3 pick swap was about as good of a deal as the Cardinals could have landed. Harrison ran his course in the desert and was clearly a poor fit in Mike LaFleur's system, so maximizing his value in the trade was a big win for a team that is not going to contend for anything meaningful in 2026 anyway.

The interior offensive line in Baltimore was a glaring issue last year and into the start of 2026. The Jurgens trade addressed that head-on. Not only did the Ravens find their long-term replacement for Tyler Linderbaum, who left in free agency, but the addition also allowed them to move Olaivavega Ioane from center back to right guard. The full benefits of this move may not show up until Lamar Jackson returns to action, whether that be later in 2026 or next season.

On the Eagles' side, Jurgens' exit effectively marked the end of an era for a once-legendary offensive line that also saw longtime tackle Lane Johnson and legendary position coach Jeff Stoutland enter retirement. It is a turning of the page and one that netted a couple of draft picks for a franchise that now looks destined to rebuild following a six-game losing streak. Philadelphia had been playing Jurgens out of position, anyway.

If Porter cannot fix the Cowboys' defense, then that unit might be broken beyond repair in 2026. Dallas made a splash to address its greatest weakness and has thus far seen the exact kind of individual impact it envisioned from the star cornerback, as he allowed a diminutive 39.6 passer rating and just three completions on 11 targets across his first four games with the team. Still, the unit around him is in shambles. And with Porter set to reach unrestricted free agency this offseason, this could be a one-year rental that fails to produce a postseason appearance.

The Steelers made it clear that they were not going to shell out market-resetting money to keep Porter around on a long-term contract extension. By declining to meet his demands as he sat out the start of the season, they only had one viable option, which was to trade him. A first-round pick would have been the preferable return package, but Pittsburgh received the next-best thing with both a second-rounder and 2027 draft capital. That sixth-round pick in next year's draft already vested, as it was conditional upon Porter being active for just two games with the Cowboys.

The torn knee ligaments Jaxson Dart sustained in Week 2 made the Giants desperate for quarterback help, because the rest of the roster remained talented enough to compete for the NFC East crown. The McCarthy acquisition at first came across as puzzling given his own struggles to stay healthy, his underwhelming play when available and the fact that New York already has a franchise quarterback and thus has little to gain from McCarthy potentially developing into a viable starter. But it has aged better than expected. McCarthy threw for 243 yards and a touchdown in the fourth quarter in Week 6, earned the starting job over Jameis Winston and promptly delivered a road win over the Texans to place the Giants in command of the division.

Getting anything in return for McCarthy after a disastrous start to his career was a win for the Vikings. He slipped all the way down to the third line of Minnesota's depth chart behind a couple of low-ceiling veterans in Kyler Murray and Carson Wentz and was clearly no longer part of the franchise's plans.

#2664. Darius Acuff Jr. isn't a perfect rookie, but he may be just what the Kings need right now

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The usage rate leaders list through the first two and a half weeks of the NBA season features some familiar and expected names: Luka Dončić, Anthony Edwards (four games), Victor Wembanyama, Shai Gilgeous-Alexander and Stephen Curry round out the top five, with Brandon Miller and Jayson Tatum not far behind.

However, the name below them might come as a surprise. Kings rookie guard Darius Acuff Jr., who has a 31.6% usage rate through the first eight games, is No. 8 on the list.

The only other rookie in the top 40 is Bulls forward Caleb Wilson (No. 38).

Here are the last five players to win NBA Rookie of the Year, along with their respective usage rates.

Even with a sample size that represents barely 10% of the season, what Acuff is doing will likely be sustainable, as he's being asked to do more than any rookie in his class on the offensive end of the floor. It's for that reason that his play has drawn eyeballs and why everybody seems to have an opinion — whether it's positive, negative, or maybe even somewhere in between — on him.

Is the 19-year-old guard a perfect rookie? Absolutely not. But he is just eight games into his NBA career and is posting numbers that get him in the same conversation as players like Dončić, LeBron James and Oscar Robertson.

After finishing with 22 points and 12 assists in a loss to the Lakers on Wednesday, Acuff became the fastest NBA player in NBA history to reach at least 200 points and 50 assists. It's hard to imagine he won't be writing his name into the record books across his rookie season.

As someone who watched Acuff throughout his entire college career at Arkansas, I'm not surprised to see the numbers he is putting up in the NBA. Acuff was just the second SEC player (and the first since Pete Maravich) to average at least 22 points and six assists per game in a season.

John Calipari has coached plenty of outstanding one-and-done guards during his time at Memphis, Kentucky and Arkansas, including Gilgeous-Alexander, Devin Booker, Derrick Rose, De'Aaron Fox, Jamal Murray, John Wall, and Tyrese Maxey. Simply put: if you're an elite high school guard prospect, you want to play for Coach Cal.

Acuff's season at Arkansas had him in the conversation for the best freshman guard Calipari has coached. Does that mean he's going to become a two-time NBA MVP like SGA or a multi-time NBA All-Star like the other names on that list? The jury is still out, but his college production — on both ends of the floor — is similar to what we are seeing play out in the NBA.

For starters, Arkansas didn't have a deep roster, which meant Acuff was on the floor a lot. He played just over 35 minutes per game, which is slightly less than he's playing with Sacramento right now. The same depth issues Acuff experienced at Arkansas are what he's dealing with in the NBA with his new team.

The Kings don't have a true backup point guard, which means Acuff is playing more than anybody else on the roster. When Acuff comes off the floor, Sacramento has been playing Malik Monk as the de facto point guard — a role he has filled in spot minutes throughout his time with the Kings.

Ben Simmons was also expected to be in Sacramento's starting lineup this season, where he could've taken on some of the ball-handling duties in the first and second units, but he suffered a torn Achilles days before the 2026-27 season began. That leaves Acuff, most nights, to play the entire fourth quarter and run the offense with a team full of players who can't create their own shot.

While Acuff's offensive game is as good as anybody in his class, the knock on him during the pre-draft process was his defense. It showed up throughout his time at Arkansas, but in Acuff's defense (no pun intended), he was asked to be the primary engine of the offense while staying on the floor for most of the game.

In Sacramento, it's been more of the same.

Acuff isn't a strong defender, and projecting him as a net-neutral defender over the course of his career would be a big win for his development. The offensive end is where Acuff is going to make his money. His processing skills for his age are elite and will only get better.

Acuff to Sacramento was one of the worst-kept secrets throughout the entire pre-draft cycle. The connections between his family and Kings general manager Scott Perry run deep: Perry coached Darius Acuff Sr. when he played at Eastern Kentucky in the 1990s.

After Sacramento fell in the draft lottery and landed pick No. 7, it became almost too obvious that Acuff would end up a King. The Clippers coveted Keaton Wagler early in the cycle, while Brooklyn liked the shooting upside of Mikel Brown Jr. Even though the Kings were said to be deciding between Acuff and Kingston Flemings, the former felt inevitable if Acuff was indeed available when Sacramento was on the board.

With that context, it's easy to understand why he is being handed the keys to the offense immediately, despite being on a roster that includes former NBA All-Stars Zach LaVine and Domantas Sabonis. LaVine has the second-highest usage rate on the team (25.6%), while Sabonis — who thrived as the hub of Sacramento's offense during the 2022-23 season— has a usage rate of just 15.7%.

Even with a roster that might not look 1-7 bad on paper, the Kings simply don't have enough shot creation and shot-making outside of Acuff and LaVine. The stat that stands out? Only 23 of Acuff's 189 shots have been catch-and-shoot attempts, per Synergy. At Arkansas, Acuff thrived in the catch-and-shoot department, shooting 50% (60 of 120) in that category.

Please don’t try to hate on Acuff’s shot attempts if you don’t watch the Kings 😭Directing traffic for his own teammates, & they end up needing him to create a quality shot. He’s literally his entire team’s system. James Harden type shit. pic.twitter.com/ag5MWTcWAE

Acuff is averaging 23.6 shot attempts per game, which ranks second in the NBA, behind only Gilgeous-Alexander. While that stat might pop, most of the looks Acuff is getting have been a massive improvement from his NBA debut, where he shot 5 of 24 against the Clippers.

For a smaller guard, Acuff has done a great job of getting to the paint; he's shooting 25 of 52 (48.1%) at the rim. Acuff is also getting a healthy number of 3-point attempts. He shot 44% from beyond the arc at Arkansas, but has connected on just 30.8% of his 3-point attempts so far. Rookie guards are historically inefficient, so it shouldn't be that much of a cause for concern.

Sacramento seems to be waiting on the 2027 offseason to take a step toward a proper rebuild, though the front office has reportedly been trying to move LaVine and Sabonis — the two highest-paid players on the team — since Perry took over as GM in 2024. LaVine and De'Andre come off the books this summer, while Sabonis and Malik Monk (player option) are free agents in 2028.

The blueprint for building a team around Acuff — a player who can score at will and be the offensive engine for a team — should be what the Knicks have done with Jalen Brunson. New York surrounded Brunson with 3-and-D wings, which takes the pressure off him on the defensive end of the floor. Sacramento has just one true 3-and-D wing on the roster: Keegan Murray, who is currently out with an ankle injury.

With several high-priced veterans on the roster, this will be Sacramento's short-term future. The No. 1 priority this season for Sacramento is developing Acuff so when the big names come off the books and the team has cap space, the franchise can properly build a team around him.

One popular comparison Acuff has drawn, dating back to the pre-draft cycle, is Cam Thomas. No disrespect at all to Thomas — who was one of the best pure shotmakers and scorers in the league when he played — but Acuff is by far a more advanced passer and facilitator for his age.

Acuff is averaging seven assists per game, which ranks 12th in the league. He is also averaging 12.4 potential assists per game, per the NBA's tracking data, which ranks 11th. Acuff at Arkansas was an elite facilitator despite being a high-volume scorer. Over the last few games, Acuff has been making an effort to get his teammates involved in the high pick-and-roll.

This clip from Wednesday's loss to the Lakers is exactly the kind of play Acuff is making that won't show up on the box score: he falls over while making a cross-court pass to a wide-open shooter (Monk) who missed a 3-pointer. Acuff finished with 12 assists against the Lakers, but had 17 potential assists, per the tracking data.

Darius Acuff ter 7 assistências nesse jogo é um crime federal.O garoto tá fazendo tudo pra achar visuais para os companheiros de time e nada cai.Olha isso irmão… revoltante uma parada dessas. pic.twitter.com/TIu2m3Gm1X

Let's go back to Thomas, who didn't have a game with more than four assists during his rookie season. Acuff has recorded at least five assists in six of his first eight games, including two with over 12 assists.

Acuff's passing was one of his strengths throughout his college career. He is a very good lob passer who routinely made tough cross-court or skip passes with multiple defenders in the area. While Acuff is known for scoring, his passing is underrated.

Acuff isn't a perfect rookie, but he isn't even 20 years old and Sacramento projects as one of the worst teams in the NBA. The Kings will happily trade the good for the bad if he continues to develop and post the numbers he's putting up.

We're just over one month into the season, and the Pittsburgh Penguins are three games below .500 and 15th in the Eastern Conference. This slow start could create some very tough decisions for general manager Kyle Dubas.

On the heels of a resurgence in 2025-26, the Penguins haven't quite been able to recapture that magic yet, and there's a good chance Father Time has something to do with that. The core of this team is one of the oldest in the NHL, and not even Sidney Crosby can remain an elite superstar forever.

If the Penguins continue to occupy the bottom of the Eastern Conference, Dubas will face tough decisions. He has a handful of stars on expiring or soon-to-be-expiring contracts, and those players could be very attractive to other teams. Erik Karlsson seems like and obvious trade candidate. As does Rickard Rakell.

But if there was a fire sale, would Dubas go as far as shipping out a franchise icon?

Look, it's still very early, and there are reasons to believe a turnaround is coming. The Penguins' five-on-five numbers are far better than the results indicate, and Crosby is fully capable of shaking off a slow start and hitting another level.

If things don't improve, though, things could get very interesting in Pittsburgh. As the Pens sink, here are the updated NHL Power Rankings.

#2661. Josh Jacobs breaks finger during Packers' win, will undergo surgery and could miss a maximum of three weeks

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Green Bay Packers running back Josh Jacobs told reporters he broke the ring finger on his right hand during the 45-27 victory over the New England Patriots. Jacobs rushed four times for five yards in the first quarter before exiting the game with what was described as a hand injury. Kaleb Johnson ended up leading the Packers in rushing with 68 yards and a touchdown on 14 carries. Pierre Strong Jr. chipped in with 22 yards on eight carries.

Jacobs is set to undergo surgery on his injured finger this week and is expected to miss a maximum of three weeks, according to CBS Sports' Matt Zenitz.

Jacobs appeared to get one of the fingers on his right hand stuck in the face mask of Patriots safety Craig Woodson during a rushing attempt. He says they will find a way to play through it, but Jacobs struggled to grip the ball.

In three games this season, Jacobs has rushed 36 times for 80 yards and one touchdown. The Packers actually recorded the fewest rushing yards (485) by a winning team through eight games in NFL history, according to CBS Sports Research.

With Jacobs out, it does throw an interesting wrinkle into Tuesday's trade deadline. Green Bay entered Sunday with the worst rushing offense in the NFL at 60.6 yards per game. Could the Packers be interested in acquiring Jonathan Taylor from the Indianapolis Colts or Tony Pollard of the Tennessee Titans?

The Packers' rushing offense has been a disaster, but Green Bay's passing attack is on fire. Jordan Love threw for 373 yards and three touchdowns against the Patriots, while Christian Watson caught seven passes for 171 yards and one touchdown, and Matthew Golden 10 passes for 164 yards and a touchdown. They became the fourth duo since 2000 to have 160 yards receiving and a receiving touchdown each in a game, and the first since Tyreek Hill and Jaylen Waddle of the Miami Dolphins in 2022.

#2660. How Victor Wembanyama's improved shot diet is leading him to historic heights

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

After Victor Wembanyama authored the worst shooting game of his career on opening night, a 1-for-13 showing in a loss to the Thunder, I wrote that the Spurs' honeymoon was over. It was dramatic by design -- a play on the early-season, and in this case single-game, overreactions we always get at the start of every new campaign.

But there was truth in it. Last year, everything the Spurs did was on house money. Winning 62 games. Eliminating the defending champion Thunder on the road in Game 7 of the conference finals. Holding the lead vs. the Knicks for 72% of total minutes played in the Finals. Wembanyama unanimously winning Defensive Player of the Year and finishing third in MVP voting. All prologue, no expectations.

This year, the real story starts, and we knew the benefit of the doubt would be gone. When Wembanyama laid that opening-night egg, the chatter started. He was crowned too soon. He doesn't have a go-to shot or spot. After that game, Wembanyama had no need for the critics. He was his own biggest critic, lamenting his hesitancy and overthinking, saying he needed to "go back to playing the basketball I like."

"I got no reason to be hesitant, no reason to not be myself," Wembanyama said. "For me, it's as simple as that. I'm good when I have fun."

Suffice it to say, he's been having plenty of fun since. Over his last seven games, Wembanyama is averaging 31.4 points, 12.2 rebounds and 4.3 blocks on 52% shooting. After opening 0-2, San Antonio has won six straight, with the latest being Wednesday night's 112-111 thriller over the Mavericks, who erased a 19-point deficit to tie the game with under two minutes to play.

In the end, Wembanyama was just too much. He scored the Spurs' final seven points and 11 of their last 13 and hit the game-winning free-throw. When it was all said and done, the box score read like something out of a video game: 52 points, 24 rebounds and eight blocks as he became the first player to hit those marks since Bob McAdoo more than a half century ago.

CAREER NIGHT FOR VICTOR WEMBANYAMA 🚨🤯 52 PTS (CAREER-HIGH)🤯 24 REB (CAREER-HIGH)🤯 8 BLKFIRST PLAYER WITH 50+ PTS, 20+ REB, 5+ BLK SINCE BOB MCADOO IN 1974. pic.twitter.com/lHzUhYYSTz

Actually, that's selling Wembanyama short. McAdoo only had seven blocks in that 1974 game against the Celtics. Filter it for at least 50, 20 and eight blocks, and only Wilt Chamberlain has done it, and that was before blocks became an official stat. The dude had 29, 15 and five in the first half, for crying out loud. No player in the last 30 years has registered that halftime line.

OK, so Wembanyama is a beast. We all knew this. He's going to have a lot of historic-number games. But what's interesting about the anatomy of this one is where the production came from on the floor, which has quietly been the story of his season.

Wembanyama's shot diet became one of the seminal stories of last year's postseason. He's a relatively random player on the offensive end, and there were stretches when his ability to dance on the perimeter and shoot from range was becoming too easy of a crutch. He's a fine shooter and has a capable handle; for his size, he's extraordinary. But when the listed 7-foot-4 guy who is probably closer to 7-foot-6 is camping out around the 3-point line, it's a win for the defense, particularly at scale.

We saw both sides of this dynamic throughout the playoffs as Wembanyama waffled between a perimeter- and paint-based structure almost from game to game. We saw it against Minnesota in the second round. We saw it again against Oklahoma City in the conference finals when Wembanyama dominated Game 1 at the rim only to be literally pushed out to the perimeter in the following games by Isaiah Hartenstein.

Over the first two games of the Finals, Wembanyama took more shots from outside the paint (22) than he did inside (20), a win for the Knicks, who went up 2-0. In Game 3, he flipped the script, taking 13 of his 18 shots from inside the paint as the Spurs won in a blowout.

There won't always be a direct correlation between Wembanyama's shot diet and the Spurs' outcomes; they're going to win most of their games on sheer talent, and Wembanyama is going to pile up massive numbers for the same reason. But the details matter at the highest level, and so far this season Wembanyama is operating closer to the hoop with greater intention.

Through these first eight games, Wembanyama is taking five more shots a night than he did last year. Nearly all of them are coming from inside the paint, as you can see in the table below highlighting his field-goal attempts from each area.

As a matter of percentage, Wembanyama is taking 42% of his shots from inside three feet this year, up from 33% last year. Those 5.1 dunks per game put him on pace for more than 400 this season, which would obliterate Rudy Gobert's NBA record of 302.

How is Wembanyama doing this? It's not a traditional thing where he's just posting up lower (which he isn't yet strong enough to do on demand and may not ever be), and there still isn't a specific spot or shot he is establishing as the go-to move everyone is clamoring for. It's just the intent to get down there, whether it's by rim rolls, crashing the offensive glass, or forgoing some of the settle 3-pointers for show-and-go drives.

Look at the clip below. He could've taken this initial 3, but he didn't. Instead, he got off the ball to establish himself 10 feet closer to the hoop, where he's now one cut away from a dunk as the Spurs have five 3-point threats on the floor who have collectively pulled every defender away from the basket.

Stephon Castle ⬆️ Victor Wembanyama 👽🤝🏰#NBAHighlights pic.twitter.com/NUX2JAQQ3G

That is what a concerted effort looks like. The seas may not always part like that, but Wembanyama is making it a point to occupy lower positioning more often, where he's ready and able to strike when the slightest crack presents itself. In many cases, Wembanyama is just hanging out beneath the basket or in the dunker's spot along the baseline from the start, rather than having to fight down there after he's started the possession 30 feet away.

One thing the Spurs are doing is initiating pick-and-rolls lower on the floor, so that Wembanyama, with his length, is a single turn from the front of the rim rather than having to navigate all the way from the 3-point line, which gives defenses time to clog his path.

HE'S GOT 47 PTS! 📺 ESPN, @DAZN, @CW35SA pic.twitter.com/ck0iYgngLs

This isn't rocket science. Wembanyama can go up so much higher than everyone else that it's simply a matter of him being near the rim. From there, the Spurs are just throwing it up as you would to an adult playing with kids.

Where Wemby catches the ball for this alley oop is ABSURD pic.twitter.com/azoeaeWUyv

Even the off-the-backboard lobs that Wembanyama is throwing to himself are more than a social media highlight. Note where he's catching the ball: at the free-throw line. When Wembanyama is one step from the rim, just about anything is at his disposal.

WEMBY IS SCARY 😧 pic.twitter.com/A4tPuDvQoa

De'Aaron Fox has talked about running these pick-and-rolls with Wembanyama where he's popping into the free-throw area for soft-spot jumpers, which are going to be there any time he wants as defenses sag back in an attempt, to whatever degree possible, to discourage dunks.

Those shots are about as close to a guaranteed clean look that Wembanyama can get from inside the arc. They are not going in at the moment. He's just 28% from 10-16 feet. But these are the stations from which he can play entirely on his terms. The 3-pointers, particularly the pull-up ones, are on the defense's terms, though he can make them and on plenty of nights will.

So far this year, Wembanyama is making just 24% of his 3s. That will go up, and the threat of him making that shot serves San Antonio's spacing well. He shouldn't, and won't, quit taking them. When they start going in, it could get flat-out unstoppable. But it's a fine balance, and Wembanyama is rightfully erring more on the lower side of the floor this year.

When Wembanyama scored his previous career high of 50 points in 2024, he did so on the strength of eight made 3s. On Wednesday, he only made one 3, while making 15 of his 20 shots from inside the arc. By aggressively going into the paint, he's also in position to draw more fouls, and indeed he made 19 free throws against the Mavs.

That is old-school center stuff. Just flat-out dominating inside. Wembanyama can obviously get buckets either way, but the closer-to-the-hoop way is the better bet all things being equal. On some level, this is pretty simple for a player this size, and you can see Wembanyama starting to figure that out.

So who goes where? That's for agents and general managers to figure out. We already covered Tarik Skubal, so your CBS Sports experts are digging a bit deeper down the list for a new round of guessing games.

Mike Axisa: There are already rumblings that Morejon wants to start in 2027 and I reckon more than a few teams will be willing to give him that opportunity. Dayn Perry: Any team can use a lockdown reliever like Morejon, who's also young for a free agent. He's got the repertoire to be a starter conversion, too. The Yankees could use him, of course, and I expect they'll pay what it takes.

Matt Snyder: The Cubs badly need rotation help and Wrigley Field, thanks to Chicago wind patterns, is better suited for left-handed pitchers. Mike Axisa: The Cubs have long been rumored as a landing spot for Peralta because of the Craig Counsell connection, though I like the other Chicago team as a fit better. #2658. Hoffenheim claim 2-1 victory over Schalke after early Karius error

Hoffenheim returned to winning ways in the Bundesliga thanks to goals from Fisnik Asllani and Tim Lemperle providing a 2-1 win to see them head into the international break in 9th place. The match was also marked by injury concerns for Schalke, with both goalkeeper Loris Karius and Robin Gosens forced off during the contest.

Hoffenheim made the perfect start when Asllani opened the scoring after just 10 minutes. Schalke goalkeeper Karius was at fault for the goal after attempting to play the ball out from the back, only to see his pass intercepted by the alert Hoffenheim forward, who guided the ball into the net.

The visitors responded positively to falling behind, with Adil Aouchiche going close to an equaliser in the 14th minute. However, Oliver Baumann produced an excellent save to deny the Schalke attacker after Kenan Karaman had created the opportunity.

Schalke's failure to take advantage of their promising start was punished when Hoffenheim doubled their advantage in the 26th minute. Following some patient build-up play, Tim Lemperle exchanged passes with Asllani before calmly slotting the ball past Karius to make it 2-0.

Christian Ilzer's side continued to threaten before the break, with Alexander Prass firing narrowly over after being played through by Lemperle. Robin Gosens also had an opportunity at the other end, but his attempted volley failed to trouble Baumann.

The second half began with a significant setback for Schalke. In the 47th minute, Karius produced an excellent save to deny Asllani, but the goalkeeper subsequently collided with his own defender Gosens as the latter attempted to reach the rebound.

Both players required treatment and were unable to continue. Karius was replaced by Kevin Müller, while Vitalie Becker came on for Gosens in a double injury blow for Miron Muslić's side.

Schalke nevertheless continued to search for a way back into the contest. Soufiane El-Faouzi came particularly close in the 57th minute, striking the crossbar after Baumann had initially saved an effort from Becker.

Hoffenheim thought they had added a third goal shortly afterwards, but Andrej Kramarić was ruled offside. At the other end, Junior Adamu squandered a golden opportunity in the 72nd minute, firing wide from close range after his attempt was deflected by Vladimír Coufal.

Schalke eventually found a breakthrough in the 81st minute. Edin Džeko's header was initially saved by Baumann, but the rebound fell kindly for Adamu, who made no mistake from close range to reduce the deficit to 2-1.

The late goal gave Schalke renewed hope, but Hoffenheim managed to hold on during the closing stages to secure all three points.

The result gives Ilzer's team an important Bundesliga victory, while Schalke are left to reflect on a frustrating evening in Sinsheim. Despite their second-half improvement and late goal, Muslić's side were ultimately unable to recover from their costly first-half mistakes.

#2656. Vikings vs. Bills prediction: Josh Allen faces NFL's top defense on Monday night

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

In the Week 9 edition of "Monday Night Football," the Minnesota Vikings host the Buffalo Bills. Minnesota is coming off its first loss of the season after starting the year with six straight wins. The Vikings turn to Carson Wentz to start in place of Kyler Murray, who is dealing with a hamstring injury. Minnesota sports arguably the NFL's best defense, and it will be put to the test on Monday night against the Bills.

Buffalo has won three consecutive games to improve to 6-1, and last week beat up on the Baltimore Ravens following an injury to Lamar Jackson on the Ravens' first snap of the game. Buffalo is in first place in the AFC East behind its efficient and explosive offense, which has helped offset a defense that has been highly vulnerable this year.

Will the Vikings bounce back, or will the Bills continue to roll? We'll find out soon enough. Before we break down the matchup, here's a look at how you can watch the game.

This is going to be one of the most fascinating matchups of the season, as arguably the NFL's best quarterback (Josh Allen) will do battle with arguably the NFL's best defensive play-caller (Brian Flores). We know the state of play: the Vikings are going to blitz on damn near every snap, and the Bills are going to have to figure out how in the world to deal with all the extra bodies the Vikings send against both the run and the pass.

Last week, the Vikings totally shut down one of the best offenses in the league during the first half, holding the Lions to a mere 154 total yards (on 36 plays, an average of 4.3 per play) and only six points prior to the break. They frustrated Jared Goff and the passing game with their heavy blitzing and they limited Jahmyr Gibbs and company to a 25% rushing success rate.

Buffalo has been one of the best running teams in the NFL, averaging 4.8 yards per carry, which ranks fourth in the league. The Bills can lean on James Cook, who, after leading the NFL in rushing last year, is actually averaging nearly six more rushing yards per game than he did a year ago. Buffalo likes to get downhill runs with schemes like duo that create double teams inside, which is tough to do against the Vikings, but can lead to big gains if you can block them up front. Whether the Bills can do that is obviously another question.

It's important to note that Allen has been blitzed on exactly a third of his dropbacks, per Tru Media, meaning he's faced the 11th-highest blitz rate in the NFL. He's 46 of 70 for 587 yards, three touchdowns and three interceptions on those plays, and he's been sacked six times. That's all led to him checking in fourth in yards per attempt (8.4) and seventh in passing success rate (50.0%) but only 15th in EPA per dropback thanks to the interceptions.

The Bills will need to get the ball out quickly against the blitz, which could mean underneath targets like Khalil Shakir and passing-down back Ty Johnson are heavily involved. It might be a lighter game for the likes of Dalton Kincaid and Dawson Knox, as teams often keep their tight ends back in pass protection against Flores' blitz-happy defense.

It might also be tough for DJ Moore and Keon Coleman to get open down the field, but there could be opportunities for big plays if the offensive line does hold up on any given snap. The Vikings have given up the occasional deep shot this year because they send so many men after the quarterback and it leaves them shorthanded on the back end at times.

The Vikings have struggled to move the ball pretty much all season. Their 4.7 yards-per-play average is tied for third-worst in the NFL. Their 1.71 points-per-drive average is fifth-worst in the NFL. And their -0.14 expected points added per play average is second-worst in the NFL, according to Tru Media.

They've yet to gain more than 364 yards in any game, and they've been at 275 or fewer in five of their seven contests. They've scored more than 23 points just one time, and it was back in Week 1 when they had touchdown drives of 28, 1 and 14 yards late in the game against the Green Bay Packers.

Some of the struggles can be laid at the feet of Kyler Murray, who has completed 64.9% of his passes at an average of just 6.6 yards per attempt, with a mere five touchdown passes and three interceptions. Some of the struggles can be laid at the feet of the run game, where the backs have combined to average south of 4.0 yards per carry. Jordan Mason missed four games, but it's not like he's been effective when he's been on the field, having averaged 3.9 yards a pop.

Murray won't be on the field on Monday night. It'll be Carson Wentz under center in his place. Wentz went 23 of 39 for 276 yards and three touchdowns in one-plus games in relief of Murray earlier this year. He seemed to have more command of the offense and more chemistry with Justin Jefferson than Murray does, at the very least. Jefferson went for eight catches for 92 yards and two scores during Wentz's relief appearance back in Week 1, and he was on the receiving end of seven of Wentz's 19 pass attempts in that game. (Wentz's start the following week came in a driving rainstorm in Chicago and doesn't provide much room for analysis.)

If the Vikings can keep Wentz well-protected, there should be some opportunities for Jefferson, Jordan Addison and T.J. Hockenson to find openings in what has been a very leaky back seven. The Bills have been solid against the run this year, allowing only 3.9 yards per carry. Given the Vikings' struggles on the ground, it seems unlikely that they'll have much in the way of success running the ball here.

You can't ask me to buy into this Minnesota offense right now — not even against Buffalo's leaky defense. We just saw the Vikings put up a relatively limp offensive performance against the Lions. And if there's a team out there that can run the ball on Minnesota the way the Lions did, it might be the Bills with Josh Allen and James Cook. Buffalo can win a low-ish scoring game here by doing just that.

#2655. Bronny James faces uncertain NBA future after Lakers assign him to G League

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Los Angeles Lakers assigned Bronny James and rookie Cameron Carr to the G League on Thursday, the team announced. James is no stranger to the Coachella Valley Lakers, having spent time with them across his first two seasons. Still, such an early G League assignment isn't exactly an encouraging start to his third NBA campaign.

James, the 22-year-old son of LeBron James, played for the Lakers in the playoffs last season out of desperation due injuries, but when the team has been closer to full strength, he has failed to earn more than spot minutes in his first two NBA seasons. He struggled mightily in the preseason this year, as he shot just 4 of 16 from the field. And while he has always been a defense-first player, his size -- 6-foot-2 and 210 pounds -- has limited his upside on that side of the floor.

"I thought he had a really nice September and a good summer with us, but I don't think he's played well in the four preseason games," Lakers coach JJ Redick said in October.

Despite those preseason struggles, James survived final cuts as the Lakers ultimately waived former No. 17 overall pick Dalton Knecht to get their roster down to 15 players. The move was relatively surprising considering their draft status. While both Knecht and James have fallen short of the team's hopes for them, Knecht was a former first-round pick who had at least held a consistent rotation role early in his rookie season. He fell off after a failed trade to the Charlotte Hornets, but teams typically like to give their own first-round picks as many opportunities as possible to succeed.

Knecht has since signed a two-way contract with the defending NBA champion New York Knicks. He appeared in his first game on Wednesday, a blowout win over the Chicago Bulls, and he notched 10 points in 16 minutes. By comparison, James has scored four points in 12 minutes spread across five appearances this season.

James was drafted in 2024 and became the first player in NBA history to share the court with his father. Now the elder James is a member of the Philadelphia 76ers, and both teams are doing well after their separation. The 76ers have the NBA's best record at 8-1, and the Lakers aren't far behind at 7-2. But with his father gone and the Lakers thriving in his absence, the younger James is in a somewhat precarious position moving forward. His name carries less weight with the organization than it once did, and a team with championship ambitions isn't going to be willing to wait on the development of a second-round pick forever.

James' contract is guaranteed through the end of this season, but not guaranteed afterward. If he doesn't show progress quickly, he could be a trade candidate at the deadline or simply not retained after the season.

#2654. How busy will the MLB offseason be before likely lockout? Insiders weigh in on November's urgency, uncertainty

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Hot stove season is underway in Major League Baseball. And with a lockout looming when the current collective bargaining agreement expires Dec. 1, the next four weeks will likely be the only time that teams have to sign free agents, make trades and reshape their rosters before transactions come to a halt.

Want some context into just how much of a mad dash this could become? One brief exchange with a head of baseball operations offered a glimpse. When asked what his club anticipated in the coming weeks, the executive offered only this: "I'm going to stiff arm you on this one," the exec said. "Because I'm time constrained right now. A lot going on with staff and player conversations."

Urgency will play a role this November. Naturally, teams don't want to be left behind. And the way modern baseball conducts business could be challenged.

Over the last five years, the early stages of MLB's offseason have been largely anticlimactic. Front offices, many of which rely on similar analytical models, have increasingly approached the market with caution, contributing to a process that can drag well into the winter.

Even the Winter Meetings, traditionally a gathering place in early December for blockbuster trades and significant free-agent signings, have increasingly become more of a launching pad for offseason conversations than a destination for completed deals.

So, what does this peculiar November have in store? Yes, there will be moves. But according to one high-ranking league executive, don't expect the approaches that have defined the modern offseason to change entirely. The urgency might be different, but the process of gathering information, evaluating talent and understanding the market remains largely the same.

"You can't get caught flat-footed, so we're going through the same motions of lining up who we like, identifying different ways to meet our needs, calling agents and letting them know we have interest," the executive said. "Next week at GM meetings will be helpful to learn more. That's usually when we indicate we want to zoom with a player and we'll see how agents/players react to that."

Trades, certainly, could take precedence over free-agent signings, given the circumstances and the talent available. This year's free-agent class is notably weak, particularly when it comes to starting pitching. The trade market, meanwhile, could offer alternatives that free agency simply doesn't.

One left-handed starter from the Los Angeles Angels, who isn't set to become a free agent until 2029, figures to be particularly coveted.

"A bunch of teams need pitching based on our initial sweepstakes," the executive continued. "So I think names like Reid Detmers will be in high demand. If you're a team in on him, it might be worth overpaying to jump the line. After [Tarik] Skubal, none of the starting pitching free agent names are that exciting."

No team wants to get left behind. But with the uncertainty surrounding 2027 and little indication of what next year might look like, teams don't want to overreact, either. The temptation to move quickly must be weighed against the consequences of making the wrong move.

Reacting to an opponent's moves, as that same executive suggested, can prove costly. Particularly in a market where the pressure to act could drive up the price of acquiring talent.

More importantly, all of this remains a moving target. The uncertainty surrounding the next season complicates even the most straightforward roster decisions. Rentals, as one front-office official put it, aren't particularly attractive given the circumstances. In the (still seemingly unlikely) event that there's no baseball in 2027, trading away prospects or valuable big-league talent for a player with only one year of control becomes a considerable gamble. A team could surrender valuable assets without ever getting the opportunity to benefit from the acquisition.

Years of contractual control carry even greater value now. Teams recognize that, which could ultimately stall trades. The very players who might offer the most security in an uncertain market could also become the most difficult to acquire.

"We're really operating under uncertainty now," one front-office person said.

Now, that isn't to suggest free-agent deals won't get done. In fact, one agent said he wouldn't be surprised to see a flurry of mid-tier players reach agreements ahead of the Dec. 1 CBA expiration, pointing to the activity leading up to the 2021–22 lockout as evidence of how an approaching deadline can accelerate an otherwise slow-moving market.

"Last time there was going to be a lockout it was extremely active for Kevin Gausman and Marcus Stroman, who were free agents entering 2022," the agent said.

Gausman signed a five-year, $110 million deal with the Toronto Blue Jays, while Stroman inked a three-year, $71 million contract with the Chicago Cubs. Corey Seager and Marcus Semien, meanwhile, agreed to huge deals with the Texas Rangers. A total of $1.7 billion in free-agent contracts were agreed to prior to the lockout.

This year, Sonny Gray, Tyler Mahle, and Gausman, again, certainly fit that second-tier group.

"Nothing motivates clubs more than a deadline, so I'd be shocked if there wasn't a flurry of deals prior to the deadline," the agent said.

Whether through trades or free agency, the expectation remains that deals will get done in the next four weeks. It will be a fascinating November.

#2652. Jaguars-Falcons trade grades: Jacksonville acquires All-Pro safety Jessie Bates III to bolster defense

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

On the eve of Tuesday's trade deadline, dominoes are starting to fall across the league with Week 9 largely in the books. And now, the Jaguars have acquired All-Pro safety Jessie Bates III in a trade with the Atlanta Falcons, according to ESPN. As Bates heads to Duval County, the Falcons receive a 2027 second-round pick and a 2028 fifth-round pick in return.

Bates is in the final year of his contract and is set to be a free agent at the end of this season. While this is looked at as a rental, the 29-year-old should prove to be a key addition to Jacksonville's secondary as it looks to make a serious postseason push following a 6-2 start to the regular season.

In nine games played for the Falcons this season, Bates has recorded one interception, three forced fumbles, and 60 total tackles. The veteran has also allowed a 78.3% completion percentage to go with a 115.2 passer rating in coverage, per TruMedia.

Bates entered the NFL as a second-round draft choice of the Bengals in 2018 out of Wake Forest. After spending his first five years of his career in Cincinnati, he inked a four-year, $64.02 million contract with the Falcons in the spring of 2023 and has been lurking in their secondary ever since.

Bates is tied for the second-most interceptions (28) in the NFL since coming into the league and has been named a second-team All-Pro three times, including in 2025.

Atlanta spent last offseason inking several veterans to extensions, including Bijan Robinson and Drake London. Bates was not among them, and after dropping to 3-6 on the season with a loss to the Bengals in Madrid on Sunday, they're electing to move off of the talented safety for future draft capital.

Jacksonville gave up quite a bit to land Bates. Two picks -- particularly a second-rounder in 2027 -- is a hefty price to pay, especially considering that Bates is set to be a free agent at the end of this season. I do wonder, however, whether that price indicates that Jacksonville views Bates as more than just a rental. After all, the organization does have a history of extending players that they've acquired in midseason trades. For instance, after trading for wideout Jakobi Meyers around last year's deadline, they later signed him to a three-year, $60 million extension. I'll be curious to see if Bates follows a similar path.

Regardless of whether he's with the Jags for the next few months or years, it's a great move for the 2026 squad. Bates is one of the best safeties in the NFL. In fact, he's the player in the past 40 years with at least 800 tackles and 25 interceptions before age 30. He comes in as a premier piece for the secondary, while also deepening a safety room that has been hit by injuries, most recently losing Eric Murray for the rest of the season to an elbow injury.

Give Atlanta the slight edge here. While they are losing a blue-chip player in their secondary, they were probably going to lose him anyway in free agency later this offseason.

The Falcons spent the bulk of last offseason extending key pieces to their core, and that did not include Bates. While the team is technically still in the division race despite a 3-6 record, it doesn't feel like this season will see them making a sizable push if/when they reach the postseason. With that in mind, it's the more prudent move to move off of Bates, get worse in the secondary in the immediate, but collect legit draft capital to position yourself better down the road.

Getting a second-rounder as part of this deal is nothing to turn your nose up at and is better than any sort of compensatory pick they'd receive if Bates walked in free agency.

#2651. Brewers' Pat Murphy apologized to Yankees' Brian Cashman over viral comment about Jake Bauers free agency

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

In the aftermath of the World Series championship, Brewers manager Pat Murphy was caught on a hot mic talking to first baseman and NLCS MVP Jake Bauers, who heads into free agency this winter off a career year.

Murphy's message? "You're gonna be a rich f---er, but just remember when you were on that horseshit Yankees team and you guys were all playing for yourself, just remember, say, 'this is the way we used to do it.'"

The comment, predictably, drew backlash from those who assumed Murphy was taking a shot at the Yankees. Bauers was on the 2023 Yankees, when they went 82-80 and missed the playoffs.

"I called Brian Cashman right away when I heard it got out," Murphy said on the New York Post's "The Show with Joel Sherman and Jon Heyman released on Tuesday. "I picked up a phone and called Brian right away, and had a good conversation. And the best I could try to explain that I wasn't talking about the 2026 Yankees.

"After every celebration, I'd shake his hand. I'd say, 'You rich so-and-so, you're going to leave us,' " Murphy explained. "We're not going to be able to pay you. You're going to leave us and you're going to forget all about how we did things. … I would just give him this rhetoric every time.

"I was just referring to the teams that have a lot of high-paid, long-contract players," Murphy said. "That sometimes it's harder to get all those guys together to play together. And I used the Yankees because I knew Jake was with them before. … I regret saying it, but that was Jake and I's humor behind the scenes and I got caught."

First off, dudes talking to dudes when they don't realize anyone else is listening lends itself to a lot of comments they don't necessarily mean or, perhaps more importantly, don't include the context of a longstanding relationship between a manager and his player. There isn't anything really out of line here in terms of the Yankees shot. Any Yankees fan would tell you they agree with Murphy's assessment of that team.

Where I do believe there's a problem is the insinuation that a player getting a huge payday means that he'll just start playing only for himself instead of doing things as a team. The Dodgers' high individual salaries certainly didn't stop them from winning two straight World Series titles.

Further, Bauers made $2.7 million last season, double his previous high. MLB players have a finite shelf life and need the money they make to stretch, if they're lucky, for generations. He's set to make exponentially more in free agency in his one big payday to hopefully set up his family for decades. Some might think it insensitive of Murphy to mock that a player might need to look out for himself and his family.

Then again, take note of Murphy's quote when he says that's just their sense of humor. We don't know their personal relationship because it is just that: personal. Unless Bauers signs elsewhere and comes out guns blazing against Murphy, this whole thing is probably just much ado about nothing. It would be pretty shocking if Cashman took particular offense, either.

#2649. Eagles coach Nick Sirianni denies giving his fans the middle finger after division loss: 'Absolutely not'

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The Philadelphia Eagles season isn't exactly going as planned, with a losing record and major injuries. When struggles come in sports, frustrations typically follow and Philly's head coach has been accused of letting out those frustrations with a well-known gesture after their 19-11 divisional loss to the New York Giants on Sunday, the team's first loss in Philadelphia to the Giants since 2013.

Nick Sirianni was called out for what some believe was the head coach giving fans the middle finger as he walked off the field after the Week 9 defeat. In the video, Sirianni looks at his hand, then the middle finger is raised higher than the others as he approaches the tunnel.

Nick Sirianni was asked if he was flipping fans off while walking off the field yesterday. "Absolutely not." #Eagles https://t.co/fqKylEJGxw

— Cory Nidoh (@Cory_Nidoh) November 9, 2026

Sirianni denies any ill will on whatever his hand was doing at the time, saying, "Absolutely not. That was a surprise to me. Absolutely not."

This is not the first time Sirianni and Eagles fans have clashed. In 2024, Sirianni was booed by some fans at Lincoln Financial Field, with some yelling for him to be fired during a game against the then 1-5 Cleveland Browns. Fans weren't happy that the Eagles were struggling, coming off a bye, against an easy opponent. Philadelphia went went on to win the game, though narrowly at 20-16.

As he was walking off the field, Sirianni cupped his ears and yelled at fans. At first, he said he was just "having fun" and was "excited to get the win," but then reversed his messaging, issuing an apology to Eagles fans.

"What I was really doing, I was trying to bring energy yesterday, energy, enthusiasm, and I'm sorry and disappointed on how my energy was directed at the end of the game," he said at the time. "And, you know, my energy should be all in on coaching, motivating and celebrating with our guys. And so I've got to have better wisdom and discernment of when to use that energy and that wasn't the time."

Another notable move from the head coach this Sunday was how long it took to start his press conference, with him taking the podium over an hour after the game ended. He said during that time he was talking to players and didn't reveal exactly what it was about. Typically, press conferences begin much sooner than that for a head coach, so many online pointed out the oddity.

The Eagles currently sit at 2-7 and are on a seven-game losing streak. This marks the worst start during Sirianni's time with the team. This marks the first time since 1999 that the team has started 2-7.

If Sirianni wasn't in the hot seat before (he was), he certainly is now after a bad divisional loss that put them in last in the NFC East.

#2648. Former Yankees, Rangers All-Star Mark Teixeira wins U.S. House seat in Texas

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Former Major League Baseball star Mark Teixeira is headed to Capitol Hill after winning the election for the United States House of Representatives seat in Texas' 21st district on Tuesday. Teixeira, the Republican candidate, beat Democrat Kristin Hook, a former federal scientist.

Teixeira will now take over the seat vacated by Republican Chip Roy, who didn't seek re-election.

"Together, we can build a better future for our families, our neighbors, and every community across Texas 21," Teixeira said in a statement. "I'm excited to get to work. I will be praying for all of you and for the future of this great nation. God bless Texas, and God bless America."

He was a rare win for the GOP in Texas on Tuesday, as Democrat Gina Hinojosa won the gubernatorial race and Democrat James Talarico flipped the Senate seat.

Teixeira, 46, was born and raised in Maryland before attending Georgia Tech as a big-time prospect. He was selected fifth overall in the first round of the 2001 Draft by the Rangers. He then came up through the Rangers' system and spent the first four and a half seasons of his career with the ballclub. He was traded to the Braves in 2007, then to the Angels in 2008 before signing a long-term free agent deal with the Yankees prior to the 2009 season. He finished his career with the Yankees.

In parts of 14 seasons, Teixeira hit .268/.360/.509 (126 OPS+) with 409 home runs, 1,298 RBI, five Gold Gloves, three All-Star Games, three Silver Sluggers and a World Series ring.

Teixeira is one of several familiar sports faces up for election on Tuesday. Former college football coach Tommy Tuberville won the Alabama gubernatorial race and former NFL sideline reporter Michele Tafoya lost the Minnesota Senate race.
