#2590. Six lessons learned from NFL Week 9: Arvell Reese a superstar in the making, C.J. Stroud having career year

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

With the trade deadline today, I am reminded that self-awareness is of one of the best attributes an organization can have, from top to bottom.

The team that comes to mind immediately is one we've heard a lot from -- not in a good way -- this year: the Colts. Around this time last year, Indianapolis sent away two first-round picks for Sauce Gardner in a trade-deadline blockbuster. Indianapolis was 7-2 at the time, but was it really a team that needed to go all-in? No. Daniel Jones was playing so over-his-head well, and a smart front office would have recognized the great record was a product of a very soft schedule, a little bit of luck and an unprecedented hot streak. There was no rush here. The 2025 season was supposed to be a transition one, and a medium-sized cornerback addition would have been fine. Again, just a few months earlier, Indianapolis was basically taking a flyer on Jones.

You know how the rest of the story goes. Jones and the offense start to fall off, then Jones ruptures his Achilles. Now, the Colts are 2-7 and in the midst of a franchise-altering sale while not even owning their first-round pick. If the draft started today, Indianapolis would send the No. 4 pick to the Jets. Yikes!

The Jets, meanwhile, continue to profit in a big way off of that trade and the Quinnen Williams trade. They currently own the No. 4 (Colts'), No. 6 (their own) and No. 13 (Cowboys') picks. They knew this would be a long process. They knew it could be ugly for a while, and this year's 2-7 mark confirms that. But New York could have a terrific kickstart to their rebuild in a few months' time.

One team fell for fool's gold. The other knew exactly where it was and embraced its unenviable role.

The Jets are still waiting to fully invest in their rebuild. The other New York team? Well, it has already started -- and is way ahead of schedule -- thanks to a different type of self-awareness.

Please just watch these highlights first, then pick your jaw up from off the floor and continue reading below.

ARVELL REESE COMPLETELY TOOK OVER AGAINST THE EAGLES.12 TKL, 10 SOLO, 3 SACK, 1 FF vs Eagles.Reese is the DROY favorite and making a case for DPOY consideration. https://t.co/zAwPLEFwnv pic.twitter.com/xJGzta0fCF

The biggest question surrounding Reese during the build-up to the NFL Draft was "Where do you play him?"

The answer should have been another question: "Why does it matter?"

And the Giants were exactly right to take that approach. Reese was an EDGE at Ohio State who moonlighted at off-ball linebacker. When the Giants initially drafted him, John Harbaugh basically said he'd play linebacker but also move around. Through eight games, Reese has now played at least 30 snaps at seven different spots: right inside linebacker, left inside linebacker, right linebacker, right EDGE, left linebacker, middle linebacker and left EDGE.

This is the way the NFL is trending. Think about guys such as Seattle's Nick Emmanwori, technically a safety who really plays everywhere, and someone we've talked about in this column before. Reese is of that ilk: a truly, laughably absurd athlete. A weapon who transcends positional labels. His strip sack of Joe Milton happened in 2.29 seconds, the fastest sack of the year per Next Gen Stats.

Arvell Reese Ladies and Gentlemen #BigBlue pic.twitter.com/BeoQwGZG3A

Here's where the self-awareness portion comes in. The Giants knew neither they nor Reese had to have it figured out on Day 1. The Giants are in Year 1 under John Harbaugh and defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson. Reese is 21 years old. The world was (and still is!) their oyster to experiment. Reese looks phenomenal. The Giants are 5-2-1 despite having started three different quarterbacks, and players such as Reese give them a bright future, too.

I do not blame you if you didn't watch -- or even think twice (or once) -- about the Texans-Chargers Week 9 matchup. The Chargers are unwatchable, and the Texans are middling after coming into the season with Super Bowl expectations.

What you missed and may have missed for much of this season, though, is C.J. Stroud playing outstanding football. He threw five touchdown passes Sunday, and his highlights ranged from heart-warming ...

C.J. Stroud to Tank Dell for the TD 🗣️HOUvsLAC on CBS/Paramount+Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/r0q9mBmr5d

C.J. Stroud and Kayshon Boutte with a 63-yard TD 👏HOUvsLAC on CBS/Paramount+Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/d6CjZxnTHH

Lest you think "Oh, it's just the Chargers," they've actually been decent on defense this year. This was just Stroud putting on a clinic. It's been this way all year.

The Texans' 3-5 record is mostly due to a surprisingly up-and-down defense and major struggles on the ground. DeMeco Ryans hasn't been great situationally, either. Even if Houston doesn't make the playoffs, Stroud's play is huge for Stroud himself -- he entered the year without an extension on his rookie deal -- and for Houston, which can feel much better about handing Stroud said extension.

On a week in which Jordan Love and Joe Burrow stole the spotlight, don't forget about Stroud.

I could leave it there, but I won't. Carson Wentz isn't the answer -- clearly. Kyler Murray has never looked comfortable in this offense. Is Geno Smith the answer? A reunion with Kirk Cousins? It can't be worse than it's been, and Minnesota simply cannot waste this defense again.

Jonah Coleman recorded 17 carries for 57 yards and a touchdown and caught all four of his targets for 31 yards in the Broncos' 26-21 win over the Panthers. He played 53 of Denver's 65 snaps, second-most of any skill-position player behind Courtland Sutton. He also played nine of Denver's 10 third-down snaps.

J.K. Dobbins, on the other hand, played just nine snaps overall, and zero on third down. After some injuries earlier this year, Coleman owns this backfield -- especially until RJ Harvey returns -- and that's a good thing.

Coleman already has as many rushing touchdowns (three) as Dobbins has despite having less than half of Dobbins' carries.

Jonah Coleman gets the @Broncos back in the end zone!DENvsCAR on CBS/Paramount+Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/E9pCf15J6A

Let's remember that Coleman is a fourth-round rookie, too. He should continue to get better. Denver's reportedly been shopping around for running backs, but if it doesn't land one, Coleman will emerge as an early-down bell cow (with Harvey more in the mix on late downs) down the stretch.

Just, please, Sean Payton, no more pitch plays in late-game, wind-the-clock scenarios. I think Bo Nix agrees.

We highlighted Evan Williams a few weeks ago, but that was really more about Jonathan Gannon. After a game that included an incredible interception, four pressures and five tackles, Williams gets his own slot here.

The four pressures were a season high for Williams, who blitzed a season-high eight times. On one blitz, he basically shoulder-checked Rhamondre Stevenson (a good pass-blocking back) to the side and forced a throwaway. On another, he didn't get near Drake Maye but tracked back and limited Maye's scramble to 3 yards. On his final blitz of the day, he ran right by Lan Larison and nearly got a strip sack.

Williams is a combination of a high-speed train and a bumper car attacking the quarterback. If you don't try to stop him, he'll chase you down, and when you do try to stop him, he bounces off and keeps going. He now has a ridiculous 38.2% pressure rate on 34 pass-rush snaps this season.

Oh yeah, and did we mention he can do this on the back end?

EVAN WILLIAMS OH MYGBvsNE on FOX/FOX OneStream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/0UorFkoL2o

Evan Williams, man. pic.twitter.com/HWzHimna0E

Good player. Really, really good player. All-Pro player.

It was a rough week for the NFC South. The Falcons got shellacked by the Bengals in Madrid, the Panthers lost at home to the Broncos, and the Buccaneers wasted five Bears turnovers in a loss in Chicago. The division's lone winner -- the Saints -- got an uninspiring 23-22 overtime win over Shedeur Sanders and the Browns. A failed two-point conversion is all that stood between the NFC South and an 0-4 week.

The 2026 NFC South is the only division ever with every team at least two games below .500 through Week 9. The Panthers and the Saints are 3-5, and the Buccaneers and the Falcons are 3-6. The combined 12-22 record is on pace to be the third-worst by any division since the 1970 AFL-NFL merger.

SportsLine currently does not project any NFC South team to reach eight wins. There's never been a seven-win playoff team in the 17-game era (since 2021).

But SportsLine projections also has every team reaching at least six wins, setting up for some major late-season drama. Remember last year, when the Buccaneers beat the Panthers to take the NFC South lead in Week 18, only for Carolina to win the division thanks to a tiebreaker because the Falcons beat the Saints the next day? Yeah, prepare for some weirdness.

#2589. Champions Classic NBA Draft guide: Who scouts will be watching in college basketball's high-profile showcase

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

The most anticipated double-header of the young college basketball season takes place tonight in Chicago as No. 2 Duke meets No. 5 Michigan State, followed by No. 15 Kansas vs. No. 24 Kentucky in the Champions Classic.

The event is also expected to draw a heavy dose of NBA scouts and decision-makers to Chicago, given the opportunity to see so many high-level prospects under one roof on one night.

One wrinkle: The best NBA prospect on the court Tuesday night won't even be eligible to be drafted in 2027. That's Duke freshman Joaquim Boumtje Boumtje who is 17 years old and won't turn 18 until next May. In order to be eligible for the NBA Draft, a player must be at least 19 years old during the calendar year of the draft, per NBA rules.

So not only will Boumtje Boumtje be ineligible for the upcoming draft; he is expected back at Duke for his sophomore season.

Another thing to keep in mind is that these NBA scouts and executives will use what they see on Tuesday night as a benchmark and something to measure against for the rest of the season. They will not over-index on what they see on just one given night.

The public, on the other hand, has a tendency to fall for that trap. Because tonight is so visible, if someone has a glaring performance (good or bad), it often anchors a lot of the public discourse for the rest of the season. Trevor Keels is the classic example. He scored 25 points in the 2021 Champions Classic, was mocked as a lottery pick almost immediately afterwards, ended up declaring for the draft prematurely, and slipped to the second round.

The moral of the story – keep what you see on Tuesday night in perspective, because the people who make the big decisions certainly will.

So with all that in mind, here's a look at the top NBA prospects from the four teams in action at the Champions Classic

This shouldn't come as a surprise, but the Blue Devils lead the way in terms of total NBA prospects. What's interesting about this year's team though, is that their best prospect, Joaquim Boumtje Boumtje, isn't even eligible this year, but is the early favorite to be the top pick in 2028. Boumtje Boumtje has a combination of size and skill, which is unmatched for his age, not just in college basketball, but anywhere in the world.

Ngongba had a chance to be a first-round pick a year ago, but opted to return to Duke, and so far, it looks a decision that is going to pay off. Ngonba fits a coveted NBA archetype in that he's a mismatch five-man who can play inside and out. He is a vertical spacer, reliable passer, and consistent offensive rebounder who has massive length to also be a rim protector. Scouts want to see him take the next step as a shot-blocker and as a rebounder while proving his durability.

If Ngongba can prove he can space the floor with his shooting, that's just an added bonus. He's prepared for that challenge by getting himself into the best shape of his career and looks poised to be the focal point for the Blue Devils, at least on the interior, this season. In short, it's early, but the lottery is very much in play here.

Sarr is a long and athletic big wing who, last year as a freshman, was already one of the best perimeter defenders in the ACC, if not the country. This year, he's going to get the volume to show his offensive growth. So far, that's come more in transition and as a secondary playmaker, but what the NBA is going to be most interested in is his ability to make spot-up 3s in order to fit that coveted 3-and-D archetype. Sarr was 32% from that range last season, but hasn't even attempted a three through two games this year, but has gotten to the free-throw line in high volume and made 71%, after connecting on only 53% last year.

While the progression of Sarr's total game is important, scouts will be monitoring the shooting most closely all year long. Duke also appears to be recruiting as if they expect Sarr to move on after the year. The first-round should be the expectation, with the late lottery not being out of the question.

Williams has quickly become one of the most polarizing draft prospects in the country. He was a top five recruit out of the high school ranks a year ago because of his combination of size, athleticism, fluidity, skill, and shot-blocking potential, even with real questions about his physicality.

Williams has played a limited role to start the season and could fall further out of the rotation as games get closer. Nevertheless, it wouldn't be at all surprising to see him explore professional opportunities, even if this season doesn't go as expected. It also wouldn't be unprecedented to see a team invest a first-round pick in trying to develop his tools, even in that scenario. It's a trajectory that could mirror that of Peyton Watson, who was a prized 2021 recruit who didn't play much in his freshman season at UCLA, still declared for the draft, and ended up being the 30th pick for the Nuggets a year later. That pick has gone down as a very good one.

If the exhibition slate was any indication, Blackwell may be Duke's most reliable player this season. He came to Durham after putting up 19 points and 5 rebounds on 43/39/86 shooting last year for Wisconsin, but did not get any first-round traction in the pre-draft process.

The narrative once Blackwell hit the portal was that he wanted to play with the ball in his hands. Fortunately, he seems to have gotten over that, because his path to the NBA is based on proving he can be a reliable two-way role player, not an alpha creator. Duke is the biggest stage to prove that. If the shooting splits hold up and he can provide some secondary playmaking and be a defensive asset, then hopefully scouts won't be so worried about his lack of length come the next draft cycle.

NBA scouts are also watching: Deron Rippey Jr., 6-1, freshman, guard; Bryson Howard, 6-4, freshman, guard; Caleb Foster, 6-4, senior, guard; Cayden Boozer, 6-3, sophomore, guard.

The Spartans are unlike many of college basketball's other top programs in that while they are projected to be among the very best teams in the sport, but they don't have as many glaring NBA prospects. Of course, similar claims used to be made about Villanova teams of old, and that proved to be beyond shortsighted, so it's possible that time will prove the masses wrong about the individual talent on this year's team.

Fears is undoubtedly one of the best players and floor generals in all of college basketball. Everything Michigan State does begins with him, and the same was true last year for a team that won 27 games and advanced to the Sweet 16 before running into UConn. There are, however, questions about how his game translates to the NBA. He lacks ideal measurables for the league, doesn't have the outlier burst to compensate, and is also a questionable shooter.

Still, it's hard to bet against Fears' will, and so chances are he figures out how to stick at the next level. The elephant in the room, though, is that while he is a true senior this year at Michigan State, his earning potential will almost certainly be higher in college than the pros next year. The Spartans have recruited as if he's not going to be back, but if and when financial reality hits, will they be willing to tolerate seeing him in another uniform? Only time will tell.

The baby-faced sophomore is still a work in progress and just starting to grow into his body and fill out his frame. Right now, he is much more of a Robin to Fears' Batman for the Spartans. And yet, Scott has a game that could ultimately translate to the next level more seamlessly. He's a big wing with positional size, a reliable floor-spacer who made 37% of his threes last year as a freshman. He's also a reliable decision-maker who turned the ball over a total of 32 times in 729 minutes a year ago. In short, the NBA is intrigued, so whether or not it's this year or down the road, Scott is on the right trajectory.

NBA scouts are also watching: Coen Carr, 6-6, senior, forward; Jasiah Jervis, 6-4, freshman, guard; Ethan Taylor, 7-2, freshman, center.

For the second consecutive year, Bill Self has a freshman with a chance to prove he should be the top pick in the draft. The biggest question for most of the summer, though, was based on who else they could get to surround Tyran Stokes. Now, thanks to eligibility being granted to Melvin Council, Tre White, and Tre Kaufman-Renn, the Jayhawks suddenly have an ideal supporting cast. Here's the thing, though: if those guys were NBA players at this point, they wouldn't have been available to return.

Stokes is the early favorite to be the top pick in the 2027 NBA draft. He's built like a throwback power forward, but can initiate like a guard, not just for himself, but for others as well. The biggest questions in high school were about his approach and ability to impact winning on a daily basis, but so far at Kansas, he's gotten rave reviews. Being surrounded by veterans no doubt helps, as does having some reinforcements. When Stokes dropped 27 points, eight rebounds, and seven assists on Duke in an exhibition, it was a sign of things to come. That performance came without the Jayhawks having yet established an ideal scheme to get him going in space and movement. In short, if Stokes' mindset stays the same, he has a chance to distance himself from the field this season, and that process could begin tonight.

NBA scouts are also watching: Taylen Kinney, 6-2, freshman, guard; Keanu Dawes, 6-9, senior, forward; Melvin Council Jr, 6-4, graduate, guard; Tre White, 6-6, graduate, wing; Trey Kaufman-Renn, 6-8, graduate, center/forward.

Malachi Moreno and Milan Momcilovic both had a good chance to be drafted last June. So, when they opted to return, it wasn't for a lack of options; it was for the valuation that college basketball, and Kentucky in particular, was able to pay them. That's a very different calculus than graduate students who return after not signing NBA contracts. So, while this year's roster may not have any glaring lottery picks, it does have pro talent.

Moreno fits a coveted archetype in today's NBA because he has legit size and can be reliable in offensive structure. He's a quick processor of the game and a reliable decision-maker at various spots on the floor. He's a solid passer, efficient finisher, and may even have some long-term shooting potential. He also provides some defensive rim protection, but could certainly help his stock this season by becoming more assertive around the rim on both ends of the floor. The first-round should be the goal for Moreno coming out of this season.

Momcilovic was one of the best shooters in college basketball last year, making 49% of his threes on almost 8 attempts per game, while also making 88% of his free throws for good measure. Through two games at Kentucky, he's getting even more volume, with 17 attempted threes in just two games so far. While his floor-spacing gravity is not in doubt, the questions for the next level are more about his ability to defend his position without putting his team in rotation. So, all-year scouts will be locked in on some of the nuances of Momcilovic's game, like his foot speed, angles, and rotations. Long-term, Momcilovic has positional size and a translatable niche, but may be in a familiar spot in the off-season, with more guaranteed money in the college ranks.

Wilkins was one of the best mid-major freshmen in the country last year, posting nearly 18 points and 5 assists for a Furman that went to the NCAA Tournament. He's a classic late-bloomer who had an undeveloped, wiry frame in high school, but quickly started to put things together as he grew into his body.

While he's still filling out, Wilkins is naturally smooth with real playmaking genes. Through two games at Kentucky, there's also been an early uptick in his shooting (he's 5-for-11 from three and 6-for-6 from the free-throw line). If that growth is sustainable, he'll continue to build momentum with NBA decision-makers. Exactly what his timeline will be, though, still remains to be seen.

NBA scouts are also watching: Kam Williams, 6-7, junior, wing; Zoom Diallo, 6-5, junior, guard; Mason Williams, 6-2, freshman, guard

#2588. U21 European Championship Final: English Manipulation of the German Pressing – MH

von Next Generation am 06.07.2025 in den Kategorien National Teams mit 1 Kommentar

England wins the U21 European Championship final against Germany 3-2. After just 20 minutes, England leads 2-0. This aspect analysis focuses on the reasons behind the German attacking press’s lack of access to England’s build-up play.

The U21 European Championship final offered several interesting tactical elements. This analysis focuses on Germany’s lack of access in their attacking pressing and marking. Particularly in the first half, England repeatedly managed to bypass the German press, often gaining large amounts of space in the final third, which led to dangerous scoring opportunities.

The early deficit also contributed to Germany being unable to focus, as they usually do, on securing depth in their pressing. Instead, they were forced to put direct pressure on the ball carrier in order to force turnovers. After the equalizer to make it 2-2, Germany noticeably pressed high less frequently. Therefore, this analysis examines Germany’s pressing and marking, as well as England’s build-up play, up to the 60th minute.

One of the trends at the U21 European Championship was that many teams aimed to press the opponent’s goal kicks with a +1 player on the last line or in the space between the lines just in front of the back line. Many teams—including Germany—used man-oriented marking when closing down during goal kicks.

Since most teams build up from a 1-4-2-4 structure on goal kicks, it is equally common to press man-to-man from a 4-1-3-2 shape, with the two holding midfielders (the “sixes”) staggered vertically.

The deeper-lying holding midfielder (for Germany: Martel) acts as the +1 player, positioning himself in space based on the location of the ball. When the opponent plays through the space between the lines, he can create a numerical advantage there. In the final third, pressing is carried out against a 1-4-2 build-up using a 3-2 shape. The more advanced holding midfielder (for Germany: Reitz) typically positions himself centrally and marks the ball-near holding midfielder, while the far-side winger presses the ball-far holding midfielder.

The English side, by contrast, caused problems for the German team’s marking assignments through an asymmetrical structure. As a result, England had several options for exploiting their numerical superiority in the build-up without having to immediately play into the space between the lines.

What remained consistent was the intention to establish central possession in front of the first pressing line using different players, in order to build up play on either side. Central possession makes it more difficult for the pressing team to steer the play in a specific direction, as the passing angles from central areas are wider than those from more advanced or wider positions.

Central possession complicates the opponent’s shaping of play. Anderson’s drop frees him from Woltemade’s marking shadow and creates a numerical advantage against Nebel, who must now cover both the advanced full-back and Anderson.

The asymmetry in England’s build-up play also allowed them to repeatedly exploit their numerical superiority in specific areas tailored to Germany’s pressing structure. By stretching the positioning of their two holding midfielders (the “sixes”), Reitz was forced to cover too much ground to mark both or to shift quickly to the ball-near midfielder.

Because Germany, for the reasons mentioned above, struggled to steer the press in a specific direction, Reitz was also unable to position himself closer to the ball-near player during goal kicks. Instead, he was forced to choose which of the two midfielders to mark man-to-man.

The wide, asymmetric positioning of the holding midfielders and advanced full-backs makes both midfielders available for passes, forcing Reitz to choose whom to mark. German forwards can’t shadow the opposing midfielders, while German wingers must decide between marking the spaced-out midfielders or full-backs.

England’s positional rotations during build-up play after goal kicks were most often initiated by holding midfielder Anderson. When Germany applied pressure (as shown in the diagram above), Anderson would frequently drop into the right half-space, almost into a right-sided centre-back position, while fellow holding midfielder Scott positioned himself more centrally, and No. 10 McAtee dropped into the higher left half-space.

When Anderson instead dropped centrally in front of the goalkeeper, the right centre-back would shift wide, which in turn affected the positioning of other central players and full-backs. The specific rotations of the key players, including their reference points and triggers, are discussed in more detail in the section on England’s build-up against Germany’s high pressing.

A key aspect of England’s build-up against Germany’s pressing was their ability to evade pressure through these rotations. Since Germany used man-oriented marking, they followed the English players during these movements, which repeatedly opened up spaces that England could then exploit. For example, when McAtee dropped deep into the far-side half-space, it pulled Martel—who was defending space-oriented in the center—out of position.

The aim was to repeatedly open up central areas by drawing German players out of the middle. When the full-backs, due to the rotations, were positioned deep and wide in possession, the ball-near holding midfielder would shift outward, thereby opening the central channel. This would often be followed by an overlapping run by the full-back into the half-space, allowing him to be found deep in the center with his marker behind him and plenty of space to operate.

Luring central players out of position and opening up space through rotations is one of the core principles of England’s build-up play. It significantly disrupted Germany’s ability to gain access through their man-marking approach during pressing.

Holding midfielder Anderson’s run outward opens the center, which can then be exploited by the full-back’s typical forward run.

England also added flexibility by repeatedly using long balls from their build-up play. Especially when both the full-backs and the holding midfielders were positioned deep, they opted for long passes as soon as Germany’s wingers and central players were lured far enough out. The 2–0 goal resulted from one such long ball, which was held up by striker Stansfield and laid off to the advancing Elliott and McAtee in the half-space, who now had plenty of room to operate in the open central area.

Although these long balls weren’t always as successful as in the lead-up to the 2–0, they had the effect of preventing Germany from pressing too aggressively, as players had to remain ready to cover depth in case of another long ball. For example, Martel pushed forward only hesitantly toward the dropping No. 10 McAtee, giving him significantly more time on the ball in central areas.

Against man-oriented marking systems, it is particularly important to apply intense pressure on the ball carrier, since progression is otherwise easier than against a zonal setup.

As described, England repeatedly managed to exploit their numerical advantage in the build-up. However, Germany’s pressing approach also contributed to their lack of access. The primary aim of Germany’s pressing when closing down is less about disrupting the build-up itself, and more about winning the ball in a way that immediately creates a transition opportunity.

To do so, Germany tries to use its forwards to immediately block passing lanes to the flanks, forcing the play through the third man or central passes.

Recovering possession through intercepting a pass has the advantage over winning a tackle in that it tends to allow better control of the ball and therefore more often leads to a transition opportunity. Additionally, central ball recoveries naturally result in a shorter route to goal and, statistically, in higher-quality chances in front of goal.

However, this type of pressing also means less pressure is placed on the ball carrier, since the focus is on directing play and winning the ball after a pass. As a result, England’s ball carriers had more time to locate the free +1 player, made available through asymmetry and rotations.

In hindsight, it might have been more effective to place greater emphasis on actively disrupting the build-up itself, because England repeatedly managed to bypass the German press dangerously. At the same time, Germany had the ability to control the game through their own possession, so it wasn’t absolutely necessary to rely on winning the ball high up the pitch to create chances.

Germany’s attacking pressing operated on principles similar to those of their closing down (Zustellen). From a 4-4-2 formation with a slightly advanced Reitz on the left half-space, the forwards aimed to channel the opponent’s build-up play out wide in order to isolate the wide build-up players and engage them in man-to-man marking.

On the last defensive line, Germany aimed to maintain a +1 numerical advantage, which is why the far-side holding midfielder was usually responsible for covering depth. The German wingers were expected to track back from the full-backs to press the half-backs in the three-man defensive line that frequently formed.

Even when applying attacking pressing from open play, Germany was rarely able to gain effective access to England’s build-up. This was primarily due to England’s positional play during build-up. England’s main objective in possession is to lure opponents out of position and then exploit the spaces that open up. This goal is achieved through positional rotations that make it especially difficult for the opponent to apply effective pressure on the ball carrier during pressing. The frequency of these rotations strongly resembles the rotation-heavy positional play famously associated with Paris Saint-Germain.

The following outlines the key running paths, rotations, and reference points of the most important players.

The center-backs were rarely involved in the rotations. Only when one of the holding midfielders dropped into the build-up line did the center-backs position themselves wider. Likewise, striker Stansfield provided a fixed presence in the central deep-lying position.

Most rotations initially originated from the holding midfielders, particularly Anderson. Most frequently, he dropped into the right half-space just ahead of the center-backs. This caused the right full-back to position wider and winger Elliott to drop deeper into the half-space at the level of the last defensive line. As a result, Woltemade and Nebel had to press two players, creating a 3 vs. 2 overload.

There were also occasions when Anderson dropped into the central center-back position. Consequently, the full-backs rotated into the half-spaces, or No. 10 McAtee dropped deeper. Notably, Anderson could be found almost anywhere on the pitch. At times, he overloaded the far side, which was then followed by a role swap between him and holding midfielder Scott.

Holding midfielder Scott often positioned himself in spaces that were left vacant after a sequence of rotations. Usually, Scott remained central or rotated roles with holding midfielder Anderson. It also happened that Scott took up an open full-back position when both the winger and the full-back rotated deep.

A particularly noticeable tendency of both holding midfielders was that, when in possession, they rotated toward the flank if a wide player was positioned close to the first build-up line, making themselves available along the sideline. This had the advantage of stretching the center even further.

This was especially important because England frequently won second balls after losing possession in build-up play. In the resulting transition situation, the central area was completely free, leading to several dangerous counter-attacks through the now open middle of the pitch.

Livramento, as the right full-back, primarily oriented himself around Anderson and the right winger Elliott. In relation to Elliott, Livramento always behaved in a complementary manner: when one occupied the wide position, the other took up the half-space. It was also common for Livramento to invert and drop into the deeper half-space, with Elliott moving wider in response, and vice versa.

Anderson served as a secondary reference point. Whenever Anderson dropped back to form a wide back three, Livramento either moved inverted or stayed wide and deep. If Anderson remained central, Livramento positioned himself near the center-backs in the half-space, from where he could rotate forward into depth if the outside lane was free.

On the left side, full-back Hinshelwood and winger Hutchinson rotated according to the same principles as Livramento and Elliott. Hinshelwood also frequently inverted into the deeper half-space or moved wide and deep. Both full-backs, Livramento and Hinshelwood, often initiated rotations through their inverted runs when the ball was with the near-side build-up player.

Runs into depth, however, were usually triggered only when other players moved to offer passing options. The No. 10 McAtee also played an important role as a reference point. When McAtee (and/or Hutchinson) moved into the left half-space, Hinshelwood rotated oppositely into depth.

McAtee, as a left-sided No. 10, had a freer role. He oriented himself around the holding midfielders to occupy or overload the central area when needed. He also rotated positions with left winger Hutchinson. Often, McAtee initially moved far into the left half-space to pull defenders out of the No. 10 zone behind him and then sometimes rotated further back toward the central center-back position.

In response, either full-back Hinshelwood or holding midfielder Anderson rotated forward into depth. Alternatively, winger Hutchinson could rotate into the half-space, prompting full-back Hinshelwood to rotate wider.

The English rotations created difficult conditions for Germany’s man-oriented attacking pressing. Man-marking was repeatedly manipulated, which in turn stretched and opened up spaces. Thanks to the flexibility of long balls and superiority in second balls, England’s build-up play additionally benefited in the first half. This led to repeated situations resembling counter-attacks, as England had plenty of central space available after bypassing the press.

The early goal also forced Germany to press higher more frequently and reduced their tendency to drop deep. Germany’s pressing behavior against England’s build-up thus became one of the decisive factors influencing the course of the game in the first half.

#2587. Prisco's NFL Week 10 Power Rankings: Top 5 remains same, Bengals and Packers surging thanks to MVP candidates

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

Run the ball. Run the ball. Run the ball.

That's all we ever hear about NFL offenses. If you don't run the ball, you are dead.

Let's take a look at the Cincinnati Bengals and Green Bay Packers. They don't run it well at all. Yet both enter Week 10 as legitimate Super Bowl contenders. Why? They can throw the heck out of the football.

They are the top two passing offenses in the NFL, with the Bengals averaging 285.5 yards per game and the Packers right behind at 279.7. Both have averaged over 300 the past three games.

Run games? The Bengals are 30th in rush yards per game, while the Packers are dead last. Neither is close to 100 yards per game, although their numbers are slightly up over the past three games. Neither team averages 4.0 per rush; the Packers are at 3.0, which ranks 31st in the league.

Both will have to run it better when they need to run it late in games, but, for now, having Bengals quarterback Joe Burrow and Packers quarterback Jordan Love sling it around is the way these teams need to play.

I jokingly say that neither should ever call a run play until they are leading late in games. Ok, so I'm half-joking. But you get the idea. If they keep playing with the foot on the pedal, with two big-play quarterbacks, each with a pair of down-the-field receivers, they will be tough to beat.

Both are now in my top-10 of the Power Rankings, with Green Bay moving up to No. 10 this week, with the Bengals a few spots ahead at No. 7.

Staying there for both of them will mean continuing to play the same style of football, which means not allowing the old, tired run-it folks to influence play-calling. Play to the strengths and don't get caught up in the adages about running the football.

Run the ball? Not these two. Nor should they —and both just might ride the right arms of their quarterbacks to a Super Bowl.

#2586. Bundesliga Team of the Week – Matchday 9

With Matchday 9 of the 2026/27 Bundesliga season in the books, Bulinews Editor-in-Chief Rune Gjerulff has selected his Team of the Week, which lines up in a 4-3-3 formation.

1. FC Köln may have lost 1-2 to local rivals Bayer Leverkusen, but Schwäbe certainly did his best to help his side take something from the game, making six saves and preventing 2.59 expected goals.

Making his return from an injury-enforced absence, Coufal impressed by winning all of his duels while also making valuable contributions going forward.

Another impressive outing from the French centre-back, who won eight duels and was excellent in possession, finding a teammate with 94 percent of his 84 passes.

A rock-solid performance from the centre-back, who won 10 of his 11 duels while also completing 88 percent of his passes.

Impressed at both ends of the pitch, winning 10 duels and scoring the winner in Stuttgart's 1-0 victory over Werder Bremen.

Named Man of the Match in Bayern's 2-1 win over Mainz, Kimmich opened the scoring and pulled the strings in midfield as usual. He completed 93 percent of his 98 passes while also winning six of his seven ground duels.

Leverkusen's midfield talisman scored a wonderful free-kick and completed 93 percent of his passes, while also winning six of his seven duels.

The difference-maker for Borussia Dortmund, Nmecha scored twice to inspire his side to a 2-1 victory over SV Elversberg.

Grønbæk made a decisive contribution with both a goal and an assist in HSV's important 3-1 win over Gladbach.

Although unable to find the net despite taking six shots, Kane impressed in a creative role, providing assists for both of Bayern's goals to take his Bundesliga assist tally to eight for the season.

One of the driving forces behind RB Leipzig's 5-2 win over Augsburg, Gruda provided two assists, created five chances and completed an impressive 10 of his 11 dribbles.

#2584. NFL Week 10 picks and score predictions: Lions run over Patriots in Germany, Bengals survive

If not listed, please contact your TV provider.

I just got back from the NFL game in Spain, and I think I should probably start going more often, since Week 10 ended up being my best week of the year for picks.

I went 14-1 straight-up, and yes, I should probably just retire at this point, but I don't want to retire while I'm on top; I want to retire when I hit rock bottom, which might actually happen this week. Speaking of rock bottom, I went to McDonald's four times while I was in Spain, and let me just say, I only went there because Madrid had the nicest McDonald's I've ever seen. I mean, just look at this place.

I'm now starting to understand why those Falcons players went to McDonald's. This is like the nicest McDonald's I've ever seen in my life. Wouldn't put it past Madrid to have a Michelin rated McDonald's #Bengals #Falcons #Spain https://t.co/w8WixT6iN2 pic.twitter.com/TMAeeXm9Fk

There were also people tailgating inside of a Taco Bell.

Taco Bell is in fact a mad house. NFL fans everywhere. Nothing like a pregame cheesy gordita crunch. #Bengals #Falcons #Spain #Madrid https://t.co/0uAafegmaM pic.twitter.com/cpjfyWy33X

If you need just one reason to ever visit Spain, tailgating at Taco Bell has to be it. Unfortunately, there's no game in Spain this week, so there will be no tailgating at Taco Bell, but there is a game in Germany, and it will be the final NFL game of this year that kicks off at 9:30 a.m. ET, which is definitely for the best, because I've reached my maximum limit for 9:30 a.m. ET games.

The Patriots and Lions will be playing in the early game on Sunday. So who's going to win? Let's get to the Week 10 picks and find out.

Alright, now let's get to the picks for real

Based on everything I've seen from the Commanders, I already know exactly how this game is going to play out: Washington is going to keep this thing close until the end only to lose (or tie) because no one in the organization has any idea what to do in any key late-game situation.

For instance, let's go back to Week 5 when the Commanders pulled off one of the all-time worst late-game gaffes in a tie with the Giants. Washington had the game won. All Jayden Daniels had to do was literally anything except what he actually did.

The Commanders can't get the play off in time and this game ends in a tie pic.twitter.com/WmPp6q5hU0

Look at the Giants players in that clip. They're celebrating. When the other team is CELEBRATING a tie, that means you lost.

Surely Daniels and the Commanders learned their lesson, right? Wrong. In their Week 9 game against the Rams, they needed a 32-yard touchdown on the final play, but instead of throwing it in the end zone, Daniels threw the ball five yards past the line of scrimmage because the Commanders apparently thought they were going to be able to lateral the ball to each other all the way into the end zone. That's a reason that never works.

With the game on the line Jayden Daniels can’t get the ball out of his hand. pic.twitter.com/2D8I1YWsiA

Now, you could blame Daniels for this stuff, but ultimately, it falls on the coaching staff. In the Rams' game, Daniels said he was just running the play that was called. In the Giants' game, someone on the coaching staff should have made it clear to everyone on the field that the clock has to come to a stop on that play, whether it's a spike or a player running out of bounds.

So what does this mean for this game? It means that the Commanders are actually playing decent football and if their coaching staff doesn't let them down, I think they have a good chance of winning. The Giants are beat up at quarterback, they're beat up at running back, and they're surviving by the skin of their teeth. Four of their five wins have come by one score. Good teams win close games.

To me, this is arguably the most fascinating game of Week 10. If the Commanders lose, their season is all but over, but if they win, they'll be right back in the NFC East race. I feel like this is a pick I'm going to regret as soon as I make it, but I'm taking the desperate Commanders.

With this game being played in Munich, I feel like this would be the perfect time to answer the one question that has been on all of our minds over the past few months: Who would win a beer-chugging contest between Mike Vrabel and Dan Campbell?

With these two guys heading to the beer capital of the world, there's no reason not to find out. And to be honest, based on how the Patriots have been playing recently, Vrabel could probably use a few beers right about now. I'm not in charge of scheduling events for the NFL in Germany this week, which is probably for the best, but if I were, I would rent out the Hofbrauhaus and then give both Campbell and Vrabel one full stein of beer. Instead of a coin toss on Sunday, this is how we would decide who's getting the ball first.

I was at the Hofbrauhaus once and it took me an hour to finish my beer. The Germans were definitely laughing at me.

What's the record for most beers drank in one sitting here? I think I'm going to try to break it. pic.twitter.com/UQ5kOtxyPL

The Germans might be laughing at the Patriots, too, if they can't turn things around this week. Vrabel is known as one of the smartest defensive-minded coaches in the NFL, but he hasn't figured out how to stop any NFC North teams. The Patriots have faced two NFC North teams this year and not only have they gone 0-2, but they're surrendering an average of 37.5 points per game. Yikes.

The NFC North is so good that I might not pick against any of their teams for the rest of the season unless they're playing another NFC North team. If you've looked at the NFL standings at any point over the past 24 hours, you may have noticed that the NFC North is arguably the best all-around division in the NFL this year and possibly ever.

All four teams are at least three games over .500, which is the first time that's ever happened through the first nine weeks. Oh, and did I mention that the NFC North is 20-4 against all other divisions. They are destroying everyone. On the other hand, you have the Patriots, who are 3-1 against AFC East opponents, but 2-3 against everyone else. The Patriots have had one of the worst passing defenses in the NFL over the past several weeks, and now, they have to face off against a QB in Jared Goff who ranks in the top five in passing yards per game this year.

The Lions might put up 50 points. The good news for the Patriots is that even if the Lions do put up a 50-burger, New England might still keep up. Detroit has given up the MOST passing yards per game this year (260.9), so Drake Maye could certainly get some turkey carving practice for Thanksgiving here by carving up the Lions' defense. That being said, I've decided not to trust Maye against good teams.

The Patriots have faced six opponents this year with winning records, and in those games, Maye has thrown 11 interceptions to 9 touchdowns. Based on how I think this game is going to go, Vrabel might need a Hofbrauhaus beer after it's over.

Deshaun Watson did not play in Week 9 for the Browns, but there's no chance he's going to miss this game. This is the ultimate revenge, though, I can't say for sure whether this is more about the Texans trying to get revenge on him or he's trying to get revenge on the Texans. Actually, now that I'm thinking about it, there might not be any revenge involved at all here.

Since trading Watson to the Browns in March 2022, the Texans have made the playoffs three times, and they've won their division twice. On the other hand, Watson has been injured for the majority of his time in Cleveland; he's won just 14 games since 2022, and the Browns have paid him roughly $14.5 million per win. If Tom Brady had earned $14.5 million per win, he would have made over $3 billion in his career. Do you know how many Hofbrauhaus beers you could buy with that money?

The worst part for the Browns is that they're still in QB purgatory, which is basically where they've been since returning to the NFL in 1999. Although Watson is playing well this year, especially late in games, I'm not sure that's a good thing. If he somehow leads Cleveland to the playoffs, the Browns might actually talk themselves into re-signing him, which doesn't seem like a great idea.

Anyway, this genuinely does feel like a game that's going to boil down to Watson vs. the Texans. Watson has been sacked more times than any other QB in the NFL this year (33), and he'll be facing a defense that leads the NFL in sacks (29). That's a recipe for disaster. There have only been three games all season where a QB has been sacked at least eight times: Two of them were Deshaun Watson (vs. Jets in Week 5 and vs. Steelers in Week 8) and the other one happened on Sunday with the Texans sacking Justin Herbert eight times.

Watson might get sacked 10 times in this game.

When I look back at the scores from Week 1, the most shocking result might have been the Vikings' 39-22 win over the Packers. One reason it was shocking is that I'm not even sure the Vikings have scored 39 points since that game. The other reason it was shocking is that the Packers became the first team in 12 years to lose by at least 17 in a game where they held a double-digit lead in the second half.

If there are two things I'm convinced about in this game, it's that the Vikings are NOT going to score 39 points (or even half that number) and the Packers are not going to blow a double-digit lead (and that's mainly because I don't think they'll have a double-digit lead).

This matchup will be giving us strength vs. strength: The Vikings have the NFL's top passing defense and they're going to have to figure out how to slow down Jordan Love, who leads the NFC in passing yards per game (290.9). Love is on quite on the hot streak right now: He's thrown for at least 270 yards in five straight games, which is something that not even Brett Favre ever accomplished. That's right, the young gunslinger is out-slinging the Ol' gunslinger.

Love has been hot because he has two receivers he completely trusts: Matthew Golden and Christian Watson. Those two BOTH went over 150 yards in Week 9 and they both had a touchdown. Do you know how many Packers' receiving duos have hit those numbers in the same game over the past 80 years? ZERO. Golden and Watson were the first ones.

One downside for the Packers in this game is that they won't have Josh Jacobs, but that might not actually be a downside, since they didn't have him in Week 1 and Love still threw for nearly 400 yards.

The Vikings started 6-0, but they're now in the reality check portion of their schedule: They're coming off back-to-back losses (Lions, Bills) and with the Packers and 49ers coming up, that losing streak could be at four in a row before Thanksgiving.

After spending nearly an entire week in Spain, the Bengals are back in the United States, and this time, they have to face their toughest opponent of the year: The NFL scheduling department.

For Sunday, the NFL scheduling department has put the Bengals in a situation no team has ever won.

The Bengals will enter Week 10 after playing in Madrid, and they face a Steelers team coming off a bye. This will mark just the sixth time in NFL history that a team coming off an international game has had to play a team coming off a bye, and uh, I have some bad news for everyone in Cincinnati: The team coming off the international game has gone 0-5 (and 0-4-1 against the spread). Also, NFL teams are a combined 13-1 coming off their bye this year.

And just when you thought it couldn't get any worse for the Bengals, I have more bad news: The team coming off the international trip has averaged just 15 points per game, and the ugly part is that they've been outscored 83-37 over the first three quarters in those five games. I feel like the Bengals should file a protest with Roger Goodell. I'm not sure that would actually do anything, but maybe it would guilt the NFL into never doing this to another team ever again. Oh wait, it's too late for that because the Lions will be in the same situation next week.

The problem with this situation is that the team returning from Europe usually needs a brief adjustment period. The jet lag after the flight back to the United States usually lasts a day or two, which means it can impact practice for your next game.

These two teams met back in Week 3 and the Steelers won because they exploited two weaknesses in the Bengals defense: Cincinnati struggles to stop the run (Jaylen Warren went off for 127 yards) and the Bengals struggle to cover tight ends (Steelers tight ends combined to make five catches for 97 yards). Overall, the Steelers offense simply played its best game of the season. They finished with 411 yards. They have not topped 365 in any other game.

I have a hard time seeing that happen again. If anyone can end this 0-5 international curse, it's Joe Burrow. He's playing quarterback at a higher level than anyone right now, and he's going to be out for revenge. Not only are the Bengals playing at home in primetime, but they're wearing their white tiger helmets, and I'm not picking against the white tiger helmets.

Chiefs 27-20 over FalconsJaguars 31-16 over TitansColts 19-16 over DolphinsPanthers 23-20 over SaintsBills 30-20 over JetsSeahawks 27-17 over RaidersRams 23-16 over Cardinals49ers 31-24 over CowboysRavens 20-16 over Chargers

Best pick: Bengals over Falcons. Last week, I predicted that the Bengals would score exactly 34 points and win the game in Spain and guess what happened? The Bengals scored exactly 34 points and won the game in Spain. When the Bengals left for Madrid last week, Joe Burrow wore a Pikachu hoodie on the flight over, and there's no way you're letting yourself be photographed in a Pikachu hoodie unless you're 100% sure that your team is going to win. As soon as I saw that photo, I was 100% sure the Bengals were going to win.

Off to Spain to catch ‘em all. pic.twitter.com/RLkWSboeRf

The twist here is that Pikachu isn't even Burrow's favorite Pokémon, and the only reason I know that is that someone actually asked him that exact question on Sunday.

Things you don't see every day: Joe Burrow got asked his favorite Pokémon in his post-game press conference. #Bengals pic.twitter.com/f1d4Y2rZGY

That's why we need more games played abroad. The international reporters aren't afraid to ask the hard-hitting questions.

Worst pick: Browns over Saints. I only missed one pick last week -- THIS ONE -- so I have to put this game here even though I don't even think it was a bad pick. There were at least five different occasions where I thought the Browns were going to win this, but this is the Browns we're talking about, so they eventually found a way to blow it. The one thing I didn't take into account is that the Browns' defense seems to be getting worse every week.

Everyone will understandably be discussing the #Browns quarterback situation today.The real concern for this season is the defense that continues to regress each week. pic.twitter.com/wTQfgdibRN

At the rate things are going, the Browns are going to give up 700 yards to the Colts in Week 17.

Finally, if you guys have ever wondered which teams I'm actually good at picking, I'm going to start sharing that information every week from now through the end of the season. Here's a quick look at my best and worst teams when it comes to picks this year.

Team: I'm 8-1 picking this year (Straight up): Patriots, Eagles, Jaguars (7-1), Dolphins (7-1), Commanders (6-1-1)My worst teams this year (Straight up): Bears (3-6), Buccaneers (3-6), Browns (3-6)

Every other team is somewhere in the middle.

You can find John Breech on Facebook, TikTok or Twitter, and if he's not doing one of those things, he's probably trying to round up some friends to see if they want to tailgate at the Taco Bell by his house this weekend.
